subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Legacy of Indian Removal Act (1830s): south-eastern tribes already relocated to Indian Territory (Oklahoma). Plains tribes like the Sioux retained control of their lands but westward expansion brought violent conflict. 🤠 🦅

Homestead Act (1862): granted settlers 160-acre plots in the West — directly encroached on Native lands. Transcontinental railroad completed (1869): opened West to settlers, miners and cattle ranchers — government granted railway companies land taken from tribes. ⚔️ 🤠

Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868): defined reservation boundaries — temporarily recognised Native land rights but confined tribes to increasingly small areas. Treaties theoretically recognised independence but routinely violated. 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: Native tribes still largely governed by own systems of leadership — tribal chiefs held significant authority. Federal government initially treated tribes as foreign nations negotiating treaties. BUT Indian Appropriations Act (1871) declared tribes no longer recognised as independent nations capable of making treaties. 🦅

BIA managed Native affairs — acted paternalistically and corruptly. Influx of settlers made possible by Homestead Act and railroad reduced opportunities to defend self-determination. Not U.S. citizens — 'wards of the state' with no political representation. 🦅 🤠

Reservation system: federal policy of confining Native tribes to designated land areas, managed by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA). Theoretically allowed limited self-governance but BIA agents took increasing control — often corrupt and paternalistic. Reservations were frequently on poor-quality land, leaving Natives dependent on insufficient government rations. Became template for systematic dispossession across the period. 🦅 🤠

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Federal government promoted assimilation as solution to 'Indian problem'. White Christian missionaries sent to reservations to 'civilise' Native Americans — undermined spiritual practices and replaced with Christianity. Traditional ceremonies like Sun Dance viewed with hostility. 🤠 🦅

Buffalo populations already threatened: transcontinental railroad destroyed migration patterns. Federal government encouraged buffalo hunting to force Natives onto reservations. Between 1860 and 1889 buffalo population fell from 30 million to less than 1,000. Natives dependent on poor-quality government rations. ⚔️ 🤠

heading: Plains Wars 1854–1877
summary: The Plains Wars saw repeated cycles of treaty, violation and violent dispossession. Native military victories were short-lived — federal force ultimately confined all Plains tribes to reservations.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Sand Creek Massacre (1864): Colorado militia killed over 150 peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho — demonstrated instability of frontier with inexperienced militia. Red Cloud's War (1866–8): Sioux defeated U.S. Army — forced Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868) recognising Sioux control of Black Hills. Victory short-lived. ⚔️ 🏹

Battle of Little Bighorn (1876): Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated Custer and 200 men — rare Native victory. BUT prompted harsh U.S. response — Black Hills seized 1877 in violation of Fort Laramie Treaty. By end of Plains Wars, over 70 Native tribes relocated to reservations. ⚔️ 🏹 🦅

U.S. Army killed estimated 10 million buffalo 1865–1883 — direct attack on cultural practices and food supply. Forced Natives onto reservations through starvation. By 1870, over 30,000 troops stationed across the West curtailing Native autonomy. ⚔️

Long Walk of the Navajo (1864–66): U.S. Army under Kit Carson destroyed Navajo crops and livestock — forced 8,000–9,000 Navajo on 300-mile march to Bosque Redondo reservation in New Mexico. Thousands died from starvation, exposure and disease. Treaty of 1868 allowed Navajo to return to ancestral lands — one of the few treaty victories. ⚔️ 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: Civil War (1861–5): reduced U.S. military presence on frontier — allowed tribes to engage in more conflict with settlers. BUT some southern tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw) allied with Confederacy — deepened divisions and led to forced relocation post-war. 🏹 💥

Indian Appropriations Act (1871): ended tribes' independent status — designated as wards of the state, reducing capacity for self-determination. Federal government no longer recognised treaties, removing last legal protections. 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Buffalo extermination destroyed the cultural, spiritual and economic foundation of Plains tribes — buffalo central to food, clothing and religious practices. Confinement to reservations removed traditional roles of hunting and tribal leadership. 🤠 ⚔️

Manifest Destiny: ideology that white American settlement of the continent from coast to coast was divinely ordained and inevitable — used to justify dispossession of Native lands, forced removal and cultural destruction. Social Darwinism framed Natives as 'backward' and incapable of self-governance. Underpinned all federal policy from Plains Wars through Dawes Act. 🤠

heading: Gilded Age c.1877–1905
summary: The Gilded Age brought systematic legal dispossession through the Dawes Act and Curtis Act, violent suppression of cultural resistance at Wounded Knee, and the establishment of assimilationist boarding schools.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Dawes Severalty Act (1887): divided communal tribal lands into individual 160-acre allotments — unallocated land sold to white settlers. Native-owned land fell from 156 million acres (1881) to 78 million acres by 1890. Curtis Act (1898): extended Dawes Act to Five Civilised Tribes. Dead Indian Act (1902): allowed Native Americans to sell inherited land — accelerated land loss. 🦅 🤠

By 1900, only 100,000 of estimated 240,000 Plains Indians remained — living in poverty with no resources. Late 1880s: government cut meat subsidies to Sioux reservations where disease had already killed cattle. Lone Wolf v Hitchcock (1903): Supreme Court upheld federal authority to break treaties. 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: Dawes Act undermined tribal governance — broke up communal landholding, allocated land to male heads of families, imposing non-Native social structure. Cherokee Nation v Hitchcock (1902): Supreme Court ruled Congress had plenary authority over Native affairs — eroded tribal sovereignty. 🦅

Muskogee Convention (1905): Five Civilised Tribes proposed all-Native state of Sequoyah — rejected by Congress. Oklahoma created instead. Crow Dog Case (1883): Supreme Court recognised tribal authority over criminal cases — but motivated Congress to pass Major Crimes Act (1885) limiting tribal sovereignty. 🏹 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Boarding schools: Carlisle Indian Industrial School (Pennsylvania, 1879) — over 100,000 children forced into schools by early 1900s. Forbidden to speak languages, practice traditions or wear traditional clothing. Death rates from neglect, abuse and malnutrition 30–50%. By 1930, 75% of Native American languages had been lost. 🦅 🤠

Ghost Dance Movement (1889): religious revival combining traditional beliefs with hope of restoring lost lands — attracted thousands. Wounded Knee Massacre (1890): U.S. Army killed over 250 Lakota men, women and children — violent suppression of cultural resistance. Polygamy outlawed, buffalo hunting banned, Sun Dance suppressed. ⚔️ 🦅

heading: 1910s–1932
summary: The early 20th century saw the first national Native organisations emerge, wartime service that brought no reciprocal rights, citizenship granted but undermined by state laws, and the Meriam Report exposing the scale of federal failure.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land and Self-Determination
facts: SAI (Society of American Indians, 1911): first national Native-led rights organisation — advocated for citizenship, education and unity. BUT focused on assimilation and had limited support from reservation communities. 🤝

Indian Citizenship Act (1924): granted U.S. citizenship to all Native Americans — but two-thirds had already gained citizenship through previous policies. Many states imposed restrictive voting laws, limiting political participation. Harrison v Laveen (1948) later challenged state-level discrimination. 🦅

AIDA (1923): formed by John Collier — protected Native lands and religious freedom. Successfully blocked Leavitt Bill (1926) which sought to ban traditional Native dances. Meriam Report (1928): exposed failings of federal policies, criticised allotment and poor reservation conditions — called for reform in education, healthcare and land management. 🤠 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Boarding schools housed more than 60,000 Native American children by 1930 — imposed Western cultural norms, forcing abandonment of languages and traditions. Less than 5% of Native Americans in higher education by 1930. 🦅 🤠

WWI: around 12,000 Native Americans served — many in segregated units despite not having full citizenship. Some 400 awarded Medal of Honor. Service raised social status but brought no improvement in rights. Government used wartime patriotism to push further assimilation. ⚔️

subheadings.label: Depression and Position by 1932
facts: Great Depression: already impoverished reservations devastated further. By 1932 two-thirds of Native American land had been lost since Dawes Act. Per capita income on reservations less than half national average. 82% of Native Americans still living below poverty line by 1940. Assimilationist policies remained dominant — practices like ceremonial dances and traditional religious rites banned or criminalised. 💰 🦅

heading: New Deal 1933–1941
summary: The Indian Reorganization Act (1934) marked a significant ideological shift — ending allotment, restoring some lands and encouraging self-governance. But Collier's paternalism and the limits of funding meant deep poverty persisted.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Wheeler-Howard Act/IRA (1934): halted Dawes Act allotment — recovered unallocated land, restored 4 million acres to tribal ownership (though far less than 90 million lost). Protected Native land from further sale. Tribal corporations established to manage resources. 🦅 🤠

Federal funds for buying back lost tribal land only $2 million annually — insufficient. Navajo rejected IRA due to government-imposed livestock reductions — forced killing of 150,000 sheep 1933–6, severely damaging economy. 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: IRA: allowed tribes to establish democratic constitutions and elect tribal councils — tribal councils reinstated as leaders of reservations. Out of 252 tribes that voted, 174 accepted, only 92 adopted tribal constitutions. Over 25% rejected IRA outright. 🦅 🤝

Collier's policies heavily influenced by experience with Pueblos and Navajos — did not suit all tribes. Secret ballot system alienated many who preferred traditional open council discussions. Paternalistic attitude persisted. NCAI (1944): founded to oppose termination policies and advocate for Native rights. 🤠 🤝

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: IRA overturned bans on ceremonial dances and protected use of peyote for religious purposes. Funding for cultural education increased by 65% between 1935 and 1940. Native American arts and crafts revived through Indian Arts and Crafts Board (1935). 🦅 🤠

IECW/CCC-ID: employed 85,000 Native Americans 1933–42 — planted 25 million trees and built 6,500 miles of road on tribal lands. Surplus army clothing distributed, hospitals and schools built. BUT 82% of Native Americans still below poverty line by 1940. Navajo students received only 13 cents/day for lunch vs recommended 50 cents. 🦅 💰

heading: WWII and Post-War 1941–1953
summary: WWII brought significant Native military service and temporary economic improvement — but post-war termination policy reversed gains and promoted the most aggressive assimilation since the Dawes Act.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land and Self-Determination
facts: WWII: over 44,000 Native Americans served — Navajo Code Talkers (400–500) created unbreakable code in Pacific theatre. Ira Hayes (Pima): one of six photographed raising flag at Iwo Jima — upon returning home faced alcoholism and discrimination. Service did not lead to rights improvements. ⚔️ 🏹

Japanese American internment: over 120,000 Japanese Americans relocated — some camps placed on Native reservations without tribal consultation. NCAI (1944) founded to resist termination. Indian Claims Commission (1946–78): tribes could seek compensation — awarded $800 million but no land returned. 🦅 🤝
Harrison v Laveen (1948): Supreme Court recognised Native Americans' right to vote — challenged state-level discrimination. BUT many states still imposed restrictive voting laws. 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Navajo Code Talkers' success did not lead to recognition of Native cultural rights or legal protections. Post-war: renewed emphasis on assimilation — boarding schools continued. Federal government pushed Natives towards mainstream American culture. ⚔️ 🦅

heading: Termination Era 1953–1968
summary: Termination policy (1953) was the most damaging federal policy since the Dawes Act — ending recognition of 109 tribes, destroying economic bases and accelerating relocation to cities. Native resistance began to build.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land and Self-Determination
facts: Termination Policy (1953–68): ended federal recognition for 109 tribes — sold their lands, terminated government services. Resulted in extreme poverty. Menominee tribe: recognised as successful self-governing tribe — terminated, lost land and healthcare overnight. 🦅

Indian Relocation Act (1956): encouraged Native Americans to move to cities for jobs — while some thrived, many ended up in poverty and disconnected from cultural communities. Per capita income on reservations less than half national average. Unemployment on reservations often exceeded 50%, sometimes approaching 80%. 🦅 💰

Indian Claims Commission: compensated for land losses but no land returned. Growing resistance — NCAI lobbied against termination. NIYC (National Indian Youth Council, 1961): grassroots activism — fish-ins (1960s) protested restrictions on treaty-protected fishing rights. 🤝 🏹

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: 'Forgotten Americans' speech (1968): LBJ described Native Americans as 'the most deprived and forgotten group' — launched War on Poverty policies addressing housing, healthcare and education on reservations. Shift in federal attitude beginning. Indian Civil Rights Act (1968): extended some constitutional rights to Native Americans under tribal governments — sovereignty concerns remained. 🦅 🤠

heading: Red Power 1968–1975
summary: Red Power brought unprecedented national attention to Native rights through militant direct action — AIM's occupations drew on Black Power tactics and forced federal policy shifts, but produced more symbolic than structural change.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land and Self-Determination
facts: AIM (American Indian Movement, 1968): militant group advocating for Native sovereignty through protests and direct action. Alcatraz Occupation (1969–71): led by Richard Oakes — occupied Alcatraz for 19 months claiming 1868 treaty provision. Offered $24 in beads — symbolic demand for sovereignty. 10,000 Natives visited. Ultimately ended without policy changes. 🏹 🤝

Trail of Broken Treaties (1972): nationwide caravan to Washington DC — occupied BIA headquarters, issued 20-point manifesto demanding treaty enforcement, self-determination and land restoration. Wounded Knee Occupation (1973): 71-day standoff — demanded sovereignty, exposed Pine Ridge Reservation corruption. Gained international attention but led to violent clashes. 🏹 🤝

Nixon ended Termination Policy (1970): formally ended federal termination, advocated for self-determination — reforms in tribal governance and federal relations followed. NARF (1970): legal representation for tribes — significant victories including Fisher v Montana (1976). 🦅 🤝

Oneida v Oneida and Madison Counties (1974): Supreme Court ruled Oneida Nation could sue for land claims under treaties — established precedent for tribes seeking legal restitution for lost lands. Showed legal route could complement militant protest. 🦅 🤝

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: AIM revived traditional ceremonies — sweat lodges — and cultural practices. Advocated for protection of sacred sites including Taos Blue Lake. Red Power emphasised cultural pride — inspired young activists to embrace heritage. AIM adopted red berets and black leather jackets modelled on Black Panthers. 🏹 🤝

heading: Self-Determination Era 1975–1992
summary: The Self-Determination Era produced significant legislative and legal gains — but poverty, land loss and inadequate federal funding meant structural inequalities persisted to 1992.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land and Self-Determination
facts: Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (1975): allowed tribes greater control over federal funding and programmes — over 200 tribes had responsibility for federal programmes by 1992. Bryan v Itasca County (1976): states cannot impose taxes on reservations — supported tribal sovereignty. 🦅 🤝

US v Sioux Nation (1980): Supreme Court ruled U.S. illegally seized Black Hills in 1877 — Sioux awarded $106 million compensation but refused money, demanding land's return instead. Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (1988): tribes could establish casinos — by early 1990s 150 casinos generating over $1 billion annually. 🏹 🦅

By 1992: 30% of Native Americans still on reservations facing land loss or restrictions. 60% economically reliant on federal assistance. Tribal sovereignty still limited by ongoing federal oversight. Sioux refused $106 million — showed cultural priorities over financial settlement. 🏹

Seminole Tribe v Butterworth (1982): Supreme Court upheld tribal sovereignty to operate casinos without state interference — paved way for Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (1988). Major economic breakthrough for some tribes. 🏹 🤝

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: American Indian Religious Freedom Act (1978): protected right to practice traditional religions, access sacred sites — but over 70% of Native religious leaders still reported struggles to access sacred lands by 1992. Charrier v Bell (1986): tribal rights over burial remains. Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (1990): required museums to return remains and artefacts — 10,000 items returned by 1992. Native American Languages Act (1990): recognised importance of preserving Native languages — 100+ language programmes active by 1992. 🏹 🤝 🦅

Indian Child Welfare Act (1978): prevented removal of Native children from families to non-Native homes — established tribal authority over child welfare. Fisher v Montana (1976): tribal courts had jurisdiction over child custody. 🤝 🦅

heading: Position of Native American Rights by 1992
summary: By 1992 Native Americans had significant legal protections and some economic gains through gaming — but 25% remained below poverty line, less than 60% finished high school, and tribal sovereignty remained limited by federal oversight.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Indian Claims Commission: compensation for lost land but only fraction returned. Sioux refused $106 million — demanded land back. 30% of Native Americans still on reservations facing land loss or restrictions. 🏹 🦅

150 Native-run casinos generating $1 billion+ annually by early 1990s — economic benefits for some tribes. BUT most reservations still faced limited land-based economic development. 25% of Native American families below poverty line in 1992. 💰

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: 200+ tribes assumed responsibility for federal programmes under 1975 Act. Tribal sovereignty legally recognised but still limited by federal oversight — 60% economically reliant on federal assistance. Only 50% of Native Americans registered to vote by 1992, turnout remained low. 🤝 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: 100+ Native language programmes active. Indian Arts and Crafts Act (1990) protected cultural expressions. Native American Graves Protection Act (1990): 10,000 items returned. BUT over 70% of Native religious leaders reported ongoing struggles to access sacred lands by 1992. Less than 60% of Native Americans graduated from high school — only 10% held college degrees. Life expectancy 5–10 years shorter than national average. 🏹 💰

heading: 🔑 DS1.1 — What was the impact of reservations on Native Americans during the Gilded Age?
summary: Reservations offered limited cultural continuity but imposed poverty, dependency and loss of traditional roles.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Positives
facts: Reservations allowed tribal life to continue in limited forms — sustaining cultural identity and sense of belonging. Better healthcare services available compared to nomadic lifestyle, albeit limited. Some Native Americans gained jobs as interpreters, scouts or in Indian Agency offices. 🏹

Navajo success: reservation land expanded from 4 million to 10.5 million acres. Sheep and goat numbers increased from 15,000 to 1.7 million. Population grew from 8,000 (1868) to 22,000 by 1900. Education initiatives: BIA established Santa Fe, Carson, Phoenix, Pierre and Landreau schools. Carlisle Industrial School and Hampton Institute offered vocational training. 🦅

subheadings.label: Limitations
facts: Land often infertile and difficult to farm — many dependent on insufficient government rations. Late 1880s: government cut meat subsidies to Sioux reservations where disease had already killed cattle. 1871 Indian Appropriations Bill abolished tribal sovereignty — tribes subject to corrupt and inefficient BIA. 🦅

By 1900, only 100,000 of estimated 240,000 Plains Indians remained — living in poverty with no resources or opportunities. Reservations became 'ghettos in the wilderness' — Natives dependent on government aid. Traditional roles like hunting and tribal leadership removed. Women in matriarchal tribes lost status as land given to male heads of families. Cultural Loss: spiritual practices disrupted, intimate connection with environment stripped. 🦅 🤠

heading: 🔑 DS1.2 — What was the impact of assimilation on Native Americans during the Gilded Age?
summary: Assimilation offered minimal economic gains for a few while systematically destroying Native cultural identity and accelerating land loss for the majority.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Positives
facts: Boarding schools (Carlisle etc.) gave Native youth vocational training including domestic skills for girls. Some graduates gained employment as Indian Agency office workers, interpreters or army scouts. 🤠

Dawes Act (1887): allocated 160 acres of farmland or 320 grazing acres per family head. Native landowners became taxpayers and gained rights of citizenship. Five Civilised Tribes exempt from allocation programmes until 1898. 🦅

subheadings.label: Limitations
facts: Assimilation targeted tribal traditions — polygamy outlawed, buffalo hunting forbidden, religious practices like Sun Dance suppressed. Missionary activity and forced Christian conversions eroded Native spiritual identities. Many boarding school graduates returned to reservations alienated from both Native and white societies. Death rates in boarding schools 30–50% from neglect, abuse and malnutrition. 🤠 🦅

Dawes Act: massive land loss — Native-owned land dropped from 156 million acres (1881) to 78 million acres by 1890. Allotment land often poor quality and sold to white speculators. Most failed to adapt to farming — majority sold their land, leaving them destitute. Matriarchal structures undermined as land allocation favoured male heads of families. 🦅 🤠

heading: 🔑 DS1.3 — What was the motivation of federal policies towards Native Americans during the Gilded Age?
summary: Federal policy was driven by economic land acquisition, cultural Social Darwinism and political control — rarely by genuine concern for Native welfare.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Economic motivation
facts: Land acquisition: federal policies including Dawes Act aimed to open Native lands for settlement and resource exploitation. Expansion of railroads — reservations 'cleared' land for westward migration and economic development. Transcontinental railroad completed 1869. 🤠 💰

Curtis Act (1898): ended exemptions for Five Civilised Tribes from Dawes Act — allowed further expansion into Oklahoma. Dead Indian Act (1902): allowed sale of inherited land — accelerated land loss and economic dispossession. 🦅 🤠

subheadings.label: Cultural motivation
facts: Social Darwinism and Manifest Destiny: framed Native Americans as a 'backward' people who needed 'civilising' — white settlement of continent divinely ordained — justified dispossession as progress.

Indian Rights Association (IRA, 1882): white Christian missionaries viewed Native assimilation as part of a Christian duty to 'uplift' Native peoples — religious ideology underpinned boarding school policy.

subheadings.label: Political motivation
facts: Control and Sovereignty: Indian Appropriations Act (1871) stripped tribes of sovereignty — ensuring federal authority over all Native affairs — tribes became 'wards of the state' with no legal standing.
Post-conflict retaliation: after Little Bighorn (1876), federal policy hardened — Curtis Act (1898) ended Five Civilised Tribes' exemptions from Dawes Act, allowing further expansion into Oklahoma.

heading: 🔑 DS1.4 — How effective were Native American responses to the Gilded Age?
summary: Native resistance showed resilience and occasional military success but was ultimately overwhelmed by federal force, internal divisions and economic dependency.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Effective
facts: Military resistance: Battle of Little Bighorn (1876) — rare victory. Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse killed Custer and 200 men. Highlighted Native resistance and led some Americans to question federal policies. 🏹

Ghost Dance Movement (1889): symbolised spiritual resilience — aimed to restore lost ways of life and resist assimilation. Five straight days of physically exhausting dances to connect to ancestral religion — attracted thousands across Plains tribes. 🏹

subheadings.label: Ineffective
facts: Military defeats: Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) — violent suppression of Native resistance, killing over 250 unarmed men, women and children. Ghost Dance suppressed. 🦅 ⚔️

Disunity: tribal divisions and differing responses (military resistance, adaptation or submission) weakened collective action. Economic disempowerment: efforts to adapt to farming failed due to poor land quality, drought and lack of support. Late 1880s: government cut Sioux meat subsidies where disease had already killed cattle. 💥

Dependency on government: starvation due to ration cuts, disease, poverty and unemployment worsened dependence. Alcoholism and peyote use reflected despair and poverty of reservation life. Cultural erosion systematically undermined resistance. 🦅

heading: 🔑 DS2.1 — How strong was the position of Native American rights by 1932?
summary: By 1932 Native Americans were among the most impoverished and dispossessed groups in the USA — with some limited legal gains but conditions worse than in 1865 in many respects.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Strengths
facts: Indian Citizenship Act (1924): granted U.S. citizenship to all Native Americans — though two-thirds were already citizens through Dawes Act allotments, military service or individual treaties.
Meriam Report (1928): documented shocking poverty, disease and death rates on reservations — directly triggered federal acknowledgement that assimilation policy had failed and reform was necessary.

subheadings.label: Weaknesses
facts: Dawes Act dominated federal policy — by 1932, two-thirds of Native American land had been lost since 1887. Native Americans among most impoverished in USA — limited access to healthcare, education and economic opportunities. 82% still below poverty line by 1940. 🦅 💰

Government policies remained assimilationist — practices such as ceremonial dances banned, public gatherings for cultural purposes criminalised in some states. Boarding schools housed 60,000+ children by 1930 — imposed Western norms, forced abandonment of languages and traditions. Less than 5% in higher education by 1930. 🦅 🤠

heading: 🔑 DS2.2 — How far did the New Deal improve the position of Native Americans?
summary: The IRA marked a genuine ideological shift — ending allotment, encouraging self-governance and protecting culture — but deep poverty persisted and Collier's paternalism limited real change.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Major improvement
facts: IRA (1934): protected right to self-governance — tribes could establish democratic constitutions and elect own tribal councils. Act also protected Native land from further sale and recovered unallocated land. Cultural preservation: overturned bans on ceremonial dances, protected peyote use for religious purposes, allowed Native children to attend local schools incorporating their culture. 🦅 🤠

Economic improvements: tribal corporations established to manage resources — funding for farming, healthcare and infrastructure. IECW/CCC-ID: employed 85,000 Native Americans 1933–42 — planted 25 million trees, built 6,500 miles of road. Indian Arts and Crafts Board (1935) revived Native crafts. Funding for cultural education increased 65% between 1935 and 1940. 🦅

subheadings.label: Limitations
facts: Collier's focus on self-determination unrealistic — failed to account for Native diversity. Policies heavily influenced by Pueblos and Navajos — didn't suit all tribes. IRA implementation uneven: only 92 of 252 tribes adopted tribal constitutions. Over 25% rejected IRA outright. Secret ballot alienated many — clashed with traditional open council discussions. 🤠

Federal funds for buying back lost land only $2 million annually — insufficient. 82% of Native Americans still below poverty line by 1940. Navajo students received only 13 cents/day for lunch vs recommended 50 cents. Post-WWII termination systematically undermined New Deal gains. 🦅 💰

heading: 🔑 DS2.3 — To what extent did the New Deal represent a change of policy towards Native Americans?
summary: The New Deal marked a genuine ideological departure from assimilation — but paternalism, underfunding and the return of assimilationist policies post-WWII limited the depth of change.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Change
facts: Abandonment of Dawes Act and shift toward self-governance and cultural preservation — significant ideological shift. Tribal councils reinstated as leaders of reservations, reversing earlier attempts to erode tribal identity. Greater respect for Native culture — funding for cultural education increased 65% between 1935 and 1940. 🦅 🤠

Political rights extended to Native American women — participation in domestic training programmes and higher education increased. Figures like Gladys Tantaquidgeon exemplified these changes. Collier's work influenced by AIDA experience — genuine attempt to reverse damage of Dawes Act. 🤠

subheadings.label: Continuity
facts: Federal policies towards Native Americans continued to reflect paternalistic attitude — Native voices side-lined in decision-making. Collier's presumption that all tribes sought self-determination contributed to resistance. 🦅 🤠

Post-WWII: termination policy and renewed assimilation systematically undermined New Deal gains. By 1953, over 100 tribes had been terminated affecting more than 13,000 individuals. Chronic underfunding — structural issues of poverty, inadequate education and healthcare remained largely unaddressed. 82% of Native Americans still below poverty line by 1940. New Deal's failure to fully discard assimilationist policies a profound disappointment — highlighted constrained ambitions of Collier's reforms. 🦅 💰

heading: 🔑 DS3.1 — How far did Black Power influence the emergence of Red Power?
summary: Black Power provided tactics, visual identity and ideological inspiration for Red Power — but Native American activism had independent roots that pre-dated Black Power's rise.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Major influence
facts: AIM (1968) emerged after peak of militant civil rights activism — success and visibility of Black Panther Party likely inspired similar approaches. Red Power mirrored Black Power's visual identity — Native youth adopted red berets and black leather jackets symbolising solidarity. 🏹 🤝

Black Power's focus on unity among Black communities inspired Native Americans to overcome tribal differences — Pan-Indian unity became crucial to Red Power protests. AIM adopted militant tactics modelled on Black Power: fish-ins (1968), Alcatraz Siege (1969), Trail of Broken Treaties (1972), Wounded Knee (1973). Term 'Red Power' directly inspired by 'Black Power' — themes of racial pride and cultural empowerment adopted. 🤝 🏹

Alcatraz: 10,000 Natives visited — gained massive media attention similar to Panthers' media-savvy tactics. Young Native Americans disillusioned with slow pace of change through traditional methods — drawn to radical tactics as African Americans had been. 🏹 🤝

subheadings.label: Not a major influence
facts: Native American protests had been developing before Black Power's rise — NIYC (1961) had already started advocating for Native rights and militancy. Fish-ins and other direct actions pre-dated AIM's formation. 🤝

Already clear indications of Native resistance — Indian Claims Commission, resistance to termination, WWII-era NCAI. Great Society and War on Poverty federal initiatives (Kennedy, Johnson) laid groundwork for greater recognition — this response may have been more a result of changing attitudes in broader American society than direct Black Power influence. 🦅 🤝

heading: 🔑 DS3.2 — What was the impact of Red Power on Native Americans?
summary: Red Power brought unprecedented national attention and influenced federal policy shifts — but produced more symbolic than structural change, and internal divisions limited its effectiveness.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Gains
facts: Red Power brought attention to Native issues — Alcatraz Siege (1969) led by Richard Oakes gained national media coverage, occupation offered $24 in beads symbolising demand for sovereignty, 10,000 Natives visited. Trail of Broken Treaties (1972) and Wounded Knee (1973) demonstrated more militant stance — gained international attention. 🏹 🤝

Red Power emphasised Native cultural pride — encouraged young activists to embrace heritage. AIM revived traditional ceremonies and advocated for sacred sites. Rise in calls for Native sovereignty — greater control over lands, laws and traditions. 🏹

Red Power influenced shift in government attitudes — Nixon ended Termination Policy (1970). Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (1975). NARF (1970) provided legal representation — significant court victories. 🦅 🤝

subheadings.label: Limitations
facts: Tensions between militant groups (AIM) and moderate groups (NCAI) who preferred legal strategies — divisions sometimes limited movement's effectiveness. Richard Oakes' death (1972) left leadership vacuum, difficult to sustain momentum. 💥

Alcatraz ended 1971 without significant policy changes. Wounded Knee similarly unable to secure lasting reforms. Red Power protests gained media attention but often resulted in short-term symbolic victories rather than long-term legislative or economic changes. 🏹 💥

heading: Native Tribal Actions
summary: Individual tribal resistance — military, legal and cultural — was the most consistent force pushing back against federal and settler encroachment across the whole period.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Red Cloud's War (1866–8): Sioux military victory forced Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868) — recognised Sioux control of Black Hills. Battle of Little Bighorn (1876): Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated Custer. BUT both victories short-lived — federal response intensified. 🏹

Alcatraz Occupation (1969–71): led by Richard Oakes — claimed 1868 treaty provision. US v Sioux Nation (1980): Supreme Court ruled Black Hills illegally seized — Sioux refused $106 million, demanding land's return. Showed tribes prioritised sovereignty over financial settlement. 🏹
Muskogee Convention (1905): Five Civilised Tribes proposed state of Sequoyah — rejected. Limits of tribal political action without federal support demonstrated. 🏹 💥

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: SAI (1911): first national Native-led rights organisation. NIYC (1961): grassroots activism, fish-ins — protested restrictions on treaty-protected fishing. AIM (1968): Trail of Broken Treaties (1972), Wounded Knee (1973) — forced federal attention. NARF (1970): legal victories in tribal governance cases. 🏹
Tribes rejected IRA outright where it did not suit needs — Navajo rejected over livestock reductions. Showed tribal agency even within federal policy framework. 🏹

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Ghost Dance Movement (1889): spiritual resistance at mass scale before violent suppression at Wounded Knee (1890). AIM revived traditional ceremonies — sweat lodges — and advocated for sacred sites. 500th anniversary Columbus protests (1992) showed continued cultural resistance. 🏹

heading: Pan-Tribal Unity and Pressure Groups
summary: Pan-tribal unity overcame the division that had weakened individual tribal resistance — from NCAI's legal lobbying to AIM's militant direct action, collective action produced the most significant gains.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land and Self-Determination
facts: NCAI (1944): lobbied for Indian Claims Commission (1946) — allowed tribes to claim compensation for lost lands. Resisted termination policies through political lobbying. 🤝

AIM (1968): brought tribes together for Alcatraz, Trail of Broken Treaties and Wounded Knee — Pan-Indian unity overcame tribal differences. NARF (1970): legal representation across tribes — Fisher v Montana (1976), Bryan v Itasca County (1976). Red Power's Pan-Indian identity inspired by Black Power's cross-community unity model. 🤝

NIYC (1961): fish-ins across Pacific Northwest tribes — demonstrated collective treaty rights enforcement. Indian Self-Determination Act (1975): 200+ tribes collectively assumed control of federal programmes by 1992. 🤝

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: AIM revived traditional ceremonies and culture across tribal lines — sweat lodges, traditional dress, Native languages. Pan-Indian identity created new forms of cultural solidarity that transcended individual tribal traditions. 🤝
100+ Native language programmes active by 1992 — product of collective cultural advocacy. Indian Arts and Crafts Act (1990) protected cultural expressions across all tribes. 🤝

heading: White Attitudes and Pressure Groups
summary: White attitudes shifted from 19th century paternalistic assimilation to 20th century reform advocacy — Collier's AIDA and the Meriam Report were pivotal, but non-Native pressure groups often pursued Native rights without Native input.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: IRA (1882): advocated for Native landownership to 'protect' their interests — but supported Dawes Act allotment which fragmented tribal lands. Believed assimilation and private ownership were in Native best interests — paternalistic and damaging. 🤠
AAIA (1922): opposed sale of Native lands and fought to preserve territories — efforts aligned with Native campaigns against termination in 1950s–60s. 🤠

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: IRA and similar groups worked with BIA to enforce assimilation programmes — undermined Native self-determination despite advocacy intentions. 🤠

AIDA (1923): John Collier — opposed government policies like Leavitt Bill, mobilised public opinion. Collier's work directly influenced Wheeler-Howard Act (1934) — restored some tribal self-governance. Later as Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Collier drove IRA but presumed all tribes wanted same form of self-determination. 🤠 🦅

Helen Hunt Jackson: 'A Century of Dishonor' (1881) — exposed U.S. mistreatment of Native Americans, sparked calls for reform. Meriam Report (1928): exposed failings of federal policies, criticised allotment and poor conditions — directly contributed to New Deal reforms. 🤠

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Missionary organisations: suppressed Native cultural practices — replacing with Christianity. IRA supported Carlisle boarding school to assimilate Native children and remove cultural roots. 19th century white pressure groups more harmful than helpful to cultural rights. 🤠
AAIA and AIDA opposed policies restricting Native ceremonies — lobbied for repeal of bans on Sun Dance. Collier's AIDA successfully blocked Leavitt Bill (1926) banning traditional dances. 🤠

heading: The Role of the Federal Government
summary: The Federal Government was more often an obstacle than an ally — systematically dispossessing Native Americans through the Dawes Act, Termination and boarding schools. The New Deal and Self-Determination era marked partial but limited shifts.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Treaty Rights and Violations
facts: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868): guaranteed Black Hills to Sioux 'in perpetuity' — violated 1877 after gold discovered. Lone Wolf v Hitchcock (1903): Congress could unilaterally revoke treaties — removed all treaty protection. Indian Claims Commission (1946): awarded $800 million compensation — but no land returned. US v Sioux Nation (1980): Supreme Court ruled Black Hills illegally seized — Sioux refused $106 million, demanded land's return. 🦅

subheadings.label: Land Allotment and Dispossession
facts: Dawes Act (1887): divided communal lands into 160-acre allotments — 90 million acres lost. Curtis Act (1898): extended Dawes to Five Civilised Tribes. Dead Indian Act (1902): allowed sale of inherited land. Wheeler-Howard Act (1934): halted allotment — restored only 4 million of 90 million acres. Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (1988): tribes operate casinos — 150 casinos generating $1 billion+ annually by early 1990s. 🦅

subheadings.label: Legal Self-Governance
facts: Indian Appropriations Act (1871): tribes wards of state — no legal standing. IRA (1934): tribes establish democratic constitutions and elect tribal councils — 92 of 252 tribes adopted. Nixon ended Termination (1970). Indian Self-Determination Act (1975): 200+ tribes administered own federal programmes by 1992. Bryan v Itasca (1976): states cannot tax reservations. 🦅

subheadings.label: Sovereignty and Federal Control
facts: BIA: managed Native affairs — often corrupt and paternalistic. Termination Policy (1953): ended recognition of 109 tribes — extreme poverty resulted. Indian Relocation Act (1956): pushed Natives to cities — urban poverty replaced reservation poverty. BUT Nixon reversed termination (1970) — most significant federal reversal since IRA. 60% still economically reliant on federal assistance by 1992. 🦅

subheadings.label: Assimilation and Cultural Suppression
facts: Federal government: boarding schools (100,000+ children by early 1900s, death rates 30–50%), Sun Dance banned, Ghost Dance suppressed at Wounded Knee (1890), 75% of languages lost by 1930. Wheeler-Howard Act reversed cultural bans. AIRFA (1978) protected religious practices — but 70% of Native religious leaders still reported struggles by 1992. Graves Protection Act (1990): 10,000 items returned. 🦅

subheadings.label: Broader Political and Economic Rights
facts: Indian Citizenship Act (1924): U.S. citizenship to all Natives — but states imposed voting restrictions. Harrison v Laveen (1948): right to vote recognised. By 1992 only 50% of Native Americans registered to vote. Reservation poverty: per capita income half national average, unemployment 50–80%, no running water in many homes. LBJ 'Forgotten Americans' speech (1968) launched War on Poverty for reservations. 🦅

heading: The Role of War
summary: War was overwhelmingly damaging to Native rights — the Plains Wars destroyed land and culture, and WWI and WWII service brought no reciprocal rights despite significant sacrifice.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Plains Wars (1854–77): U.S. military campaigns resulted in forced loss of land. Buffalo extermination (10 million killed 1865–83) destroyed cultural and economic foundation. Over 70 Native tribes relocated to reservations. Battle of Little Bighorn (1876): rare victory but prompted harsher federal response. ⚔️

Civil War (1861–5): some southern tribes allied with Confederacy — deepened divisions, led to forced relocation post-war. Sand Creek Massacre (1864): Colorado militia killed 150+ peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho. By 1870, 30,000 troops stationed across West curtailing Native autonomy. ⚔️

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: WWI: 12,000 Native Americans served in segregated units without citizenship — service raised social status but brought no rights improvement. Indian Citizenship Act (1924) partly a recognition of WWI service but undermined by state voting restrictions. ⚔️

WWII: 44,000 served — Navajo Code Talkers' success did not lead to recognition of cultural rights. Japanese American internment camps placed on Native lands without consultation. Termination Policy (1953) followed WWII — wartime sacrifice did not prevent peacetime dispossession. ⚔️ 🦅

heading: Federal Government
summary: The Federal Government was the most powerful and consistent obstacle to Native rights — through legislation, courts, military force and assimilationist policy across the whole period.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Indian Appropriations Act (1871): ended treaty-making. Dawes Act (1887): 90 million acres lost — Native land fell from 156 million (1881) to 48 million by 1934. Curtis Act (1898). Dead Indian Act (1902). Lone Wolf v Hitchcock (1903): Congress could unilaterally revoke treaties. 🦅

Indian Claims Commission (1946): compensation but no land returned. Termination (1953): lands sold, tribal resources destroyed. Even New Deal's IRA only restored 4 million of 90 million acres lost. US v Sioux Nation (1980): acknowledged wrong but offered money not land. 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: Indian Appropriations Act (1871): tribes designated wards of state. BIA: paternalistic and corrupt management. Termination Policy (1953–68): most damaging since Dawes Act — ended recognition of 109 tribes. Indian Relocation Act (1956): urban poverty and cultural dislocation. 🦅

Courts: Cherokee Nation v Hitchcock (1902), Lone Wolf v Hitchcock (1903) — upheld federal authority to break treaties. Even sympathetic IRA implementation was paternalistic — Collier presumed what tribes wanted. 60% of Native Americans still economically reliant on federal assistance by 1992. 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Federal government: buffalo systematically exterminated, boarding schools (100,000+ children, death rates 30–50%), Sun Dance banned, Ghost Dance suppressed at Wounded Knee. By 1930, 75% of Native languages lost. Despite AIRFA (1978), over 70% of Native religious leaders still reported struggles by 1992. 🦅

heading: White Settler Hostility
summary: White settler demand for land, resources and racial dominance drove dispossession, violence and the cultural assimilation agenda that undermined Native rights throughout the period.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Homestead Act (1862): 160-acre plots to settlers — directly encroached on Native lands. Transcontinental railroad (1869): opened West, government granted railway companies Native land. Gold discoveries led to Black Hills seizure (1877) — direct violation of Fort Laramie Treaty (1868). Sand Creek Massacre (1864): Colorado militia attacked peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho village. 🤠

Dawes Act allotment land sold to white settlers when Native Americans could not farm it — speculators purchased at low prices leaving Natives destitute. Economic race to the bottom: settlers lobbied government to remove tribes obstructing economic expansion. 🤠 💰

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination and Culture
facts: White missionaries: actively suppressed traditional religious practices — replaced with Christianity. IRA (1882): advocated assimilation under guise of protection — Carlisle boarding school supported. Social Darwinism and Manifest Destiny: framed Native Americans as 'backward', justified cultural destruction as civilising mission. 🤠

Post-WWII: returning white veterans competed for land and resources on and near reservations. White public opinion hostile to Red Power militancy — AIM's tactics alienated potential white allies at key moments. 🤠 💥

heading: Division within Native Communities
summary: Tribal divisions — between tribes, between traditional and assimilated Natives, and between militant and moderate approaches — consistently weakened collective action across the period.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land and Self-Determination
facts: Civil War: Cherokee, Choctaw and Chickasaw allied with Confederacy — deepened divisions, led to forced relocation. Inter-tribal conflicts during Plains Wars undermined unified resistance — different tribes made separate treaty arrangements with federal government. 💥

IRA (1934): over 25% of tribes rejected it outright. Navajo rejected due to livestock reductions. Only 92 of 252 tribes adopted tribal constitutions — shown Collier's one-size approach created internal conflict. 💥

Red Power: AIM's militant tactics alienated moderate tribal leaders and some reservation communities. NCAI preferred legal strategies — conflict with AIM limited coordinated pressure on federal government. Richard Oakes' death (1972) left leadership vacuum. 💥 🤝

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Some boarding school graduates became assimilated — returned to reservations alienated from both Native and white societies. Tension between assimilated Natives who saw some federal policies as beneficial and traditionalists who resisted all assimilation. SAI (1911) focused on assimilation — had limited support from reservation communities. 💥 🤠

Tribal differences in traditions, language and governance meant pan-tribal organisations struggled to represent all groups effectively. AIM's pan-Indian identity created new unity but also tensions with tribes who felt their specific needs were ignored. 💥

heading: War
summary: War — above all the Plains Wars — was a fundamental obstacle to Native rights, destroying land, culture and sovereignty through direct military force and the systematic elimination of the buffalo.
factorKey: 🏹 Native Tribal Actions · 🤝 Pan-Tribal Unity · 🤠 White Attitudes · 🦅 Federal Gov · ⚔️ War

subheadings.label: Right to Land
facts: Plains Wars (1854–77): U.S. military campaigns resulted in forced loss of land and confinement to reservations. Over 70 Native tribes relocated. Sand Creek Massacre (1864): Colorado militia killed 150+ peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho. Despite Little Bighorn victory (1876), Black Hills seized in violation of Fort Laramie Treaty (1877). ⚔️

Buffalo extermination: U.S. Army killed estimated 10 million buffalo 1865–83 — destroyed the economic and cultural foundation of Plains tribes, forcing dependency on government rations and reservation confinement. Between 1860 and 1889 buffalo population fell from 30 million to less than 1,000. ⚔️ 🤠

subheadings.label: Right to Self-Determination
facts: Civil War (1861–5): reduced military presence on frontier — allowed conflict to escalate. Some tribes allied with Confederacy, deepening divisions and leading to post-war forced relocation. Post-war, U.S. military reasserted control — 30,000 troops stationed across West by 1870 curtailing Native autonomy. ⚔️ 💥

WWI and WWII: 12,000 and 44,000 Native Americans served respectively — wartime sacrifice brought no reciprocal rights. Termination Policy (1953) followed WWII service. Japanese American internment camps placed on Native lands without tribal consultation. ⚔️ 🦅

subheadings.label: Right to Cultural and Religious Freedoms
facts: Wounded Knee Massacre (1890): U.S. Army killed over 250 Lakota men, women and children — direct violent suppression of Ghost Dance cultural movement. Military presence on reservations used to enforce bans on traditional ceremonies and dances. ⚔️ 🦅

heading: Position of Women in 1865
summary: In 1865 women were legally subordinate to men — no vote, subject to coverture, confined to the domestic sphere, earning half male wages in industry.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: No vote at federal or state level. Seneca Falls Convention (1848) had launched suffrage campaign but progress minimal. Wyoming Territory only exception — granted female suffrage 1869. Minor v Happersett (1875) later confirmed citizenship did not guarantee voting rights. 📢 🦅

15th Amendment (1870): granted vote to African American men — explicitly excluded women. NWSA (1869): Anthony and Stanton — federal amendment strategy, opposed 15th Amendment. AWSA (1869): Stone — state-by-state strategy, supported 15th Amendment. Split undermined suffrage movement's early effectiveness. 📢 💥

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: No women in Congress or federal office. No women in state legislatures. Political campaigns conducted entirely by and for men. Women's civic participation limited to petition campaigns and moral reform organisations — WCTU, abolitionist societies. 📢

Susan B. Anthony attempted to vote in Rochester (1872) — arrested and fined $100, refused to pay. Demonstrated women's exclusion was active and enforced, not simply custom. Minor v Happersett (1875): Supreme Court confirmed citizenship alone did not guarantee voting rights. 📢 🦅

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Women had no formal political influence. Lobbied through moral reform framing — temperance, abolitionism. Women's Crusade (1873): direct action against alcohol — precursor to WCTU. WCTU founded (1874): established women's public moral authority. 📢

No women in executive, legislative or judicial branches of federal government. Legal coverture prevented married women from independent political action. Only avenue for political influence was through husbands and male relatives — entirely informal and unreliable. 💭 🦅

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Only 3% of women attended college by 1870 vs 25% of men. Education for middle-class women framed as preparation for marriage and motherhood — not career. Working-class and immigrant women had no access to formal education. 💭 💰

Freedmen's Bureau education programmes excluded women entirely. Black women faced additional barriers — race as well as sex excluded them from most educational institutions. Civil War had created some nursing and teaching opportunities — but these were exceptional. ⚔️ 💥

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Cult of domesticity: women confined to home, family and moral guardianship — 'separate spheres' ideology dominant. Marriage seen as cornerstone of society — women married young. Divorce deeply stigmatised. Coverture: women's legal identity subsumed by husbands upon marriage — no independent existence. 💭

'Boston Marriages': non-romantic supportive relationships between women provided some autonomy in wartime settings. Civil War: 400,000+ war widows in the North alone — forced to rethink women's role. Women's wartime service as nurses and administrators began challenging separate spheres ideology. ⚔️ 💰

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Average 5–7 children per lifetime. 1 in 5 women died in childbirth. Contraception and abortion deeply taboo. Comstock Laws (1873) made it illegal to distribute contraceptive information or materials. No legal protections for women's reproductive rights. 🦅 💭

Marriage gave husbands legal right to sexual access — marital rape not a legal concept. Women had no control over timing of pregnancies. Reproductive health entirely subordinate to husband's authority and social convention. Working-class and immigrant women most vulnerable — least able to refuse or limit sexual demands. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: 15% of women employed outside home by 1870 — up from 6% in 1860. 17% worked in industrial jobs earning half male wages. Immigrant women: up to 70 hours per week in sweatshops. African American women: 40% in domestic service in the South, sharecropping common. No federal minimum wage, no safety standards. 💰

Coverture: married women could not own property, sign contracts or keep wages in most states. Civil War widows: 400,000+ forced into labour market through economic necessity — no safety net. KOL (1869) welcomed women — but virtually all other unions excluded them. Female workers highly exploited with no union rights. 💰 💭

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: Women excluded from almost all trade unions. AFL under Gompers: explicitly excluded women — seen as wage competition. KOL (1869): exception — welcomed women members and advocated equal pay. But KOL had limited industrial power. 💥 💭

Only avenue for organised action was through women's reform organisations — WCTU, suffrage associations — not labour unions. Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911) still 46 years away but conditions already in place. No collective bargaining, no safety standards, no protection against arbitrary dismissal. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Coverture doctrine: married women's legal identity entirely subsumed by husbands — could not own property, sign contracts, keep wages, sue or be sued independently. Legal framework treated women as economic dependents. No equal pay, no maternity rights. 💭 🦅

Widows and single women had more legal independence — but faced severe economic hardship without male breadwinner income. Class shaped legal experience: wealthy white women had practical independence despite formal legal exclusion. Black women faced race discrimination compounding legal exclusion. Married Women's Property Acts beginning at state level — very limited progress. 💰 💥

heading: Reconstruction 1865–1877
summary: Reconstruction brought profound disappointment — 15th Amendment excluded women and split the suffrage movement — but also produced the first national women's organisations and some state-level victories.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: 15th Amendment (1870): granted vote to African American men — not women. Anthony attempted to vote in Rochester (1872) — arrested, $100 fine refused. Minor v Happersett (1875): Supreme Court ruled citizenship did not guarantee voting rights — closed the 14th Amendment route to suffrage. Wyoming Territory: first to grant female suffrage (1869). 📢 🦅

NWSA (1869): founded by Anthony and Stanton — demanded federal constitutional amendment, opposed 15th Amendment. AWSA (1869): founded by Stone — state-by-state, supported 15th Amendment. Split damaged early movement unity. NAWSA merger still 20 years away. Black women excluded from both organisations' priorities. 📢 💥

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: No women in Congress or federal office. Reconstruction Congress focused on African American male political rights — women's rights treated as separate and secondary question. Radical Republicans sympathetic to racial equality but not gender equality. 🦅 💥

Reconstruction state governments briefly included African American men — still no women. Female political action channelled through petition campaigns, suffrage associations and moral reform organisations. Wyoming Territory: first female suffrage (1869) — only western exception. 📢

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Women's campaigns focused on 'moral reform' — temperance, abolitionism continued into Reconstruction. Women's Crusade (1873): organised movement against alcohol consumption — led directly to WCTU formation. WCTU (1874): one of the largest women's organisations of the era — established moral reform as legitimate women's sphere. 📢

No formal political influence in federal or state government. ERA petition campaigns — no legislative support. Male-dominated Reconstruction Congress rejected all proposals for women's suffrage. Women's influence entirely informal — through moral suasion not votes. 🦅 💭

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Freedmen's Bureau education programmes (1865–72) briefly expanded educational opportunity — but focused on African Americans, not women specifically. Some women's college expansion in the North. Teaching became feminised profession during Reconstruction — women entering schoolrooms. 💰

Civil War had opened teaching and nursing roles for women — Reconstruction saw these partially close again as men returned. Black women: educational gains through Freedmen's Bureau short-lived after its closure (1872). Most working-class women had no educational opportunity. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Civil War had challenged cult of domesticity — women's wartime service as nurses and administrators demonstrated capability beyond domestic sphere. Some post-war reflection on women's role. Women's Crusade (1873) established women's moral authority in public sphere. 📢 ⚔️

Post-war retrenchment: women's wartime contributions quickly forgotten. Separate spheres ideology quickly reasserted. Marriage and motherhood as women's destiny remained dominant cultural norm. Cult of domesticity reinforced by economic and social pressure. 💭

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Comstock Laws (1873): federal legislation criminalising distribution of contraceptive information or materials — active federal suppression. Contraception and abortion taboo in public discourse. No legal reproductive rights. 🦅 💭

Working-class and immigrant women most vulnerable to unwanted pregnancy — least able to access any reproductive information. Reproductive health entirely controlled by male medical profession and legal system. Women had no legal right to refuse sexual relations within marriage. 💭

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Industrialisation creating new factory jobs for women — but at half male wages. Civil War widows: 400,000+ forced into labour market with no safety net. Some women entering teaching and nursing as paid employment. 💰 ⚔️

Reconstruction Congress passed no legislation protecting women's economic rights. Legal coverture unchanged — married women still could not own property independently in most states. African American women: triple burden of race, sex and economic exploitation — sharecropping, domestic service. No federal support. 🦅 💥

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: KOL (1869): welcomed women members, advocated equal pay — but limited industrial power in Reconstruction period. AFL not yet formed — labour movement in infancy. CNLU (1869): African American union — some Black women members. 📢 💰

Male union culture excluded women — seen as wage competition. Female workers organised through women's reform associations not unions. Employers could hire women at half male wages with no union opposition. No collective bargaining, no safety standards. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Married Women's Property Acts: some state-level reforms beginning to erode coverture — but progress very slow and uneven. 14th Amendment offered potential constitutional route to equality — closed by Minor v Happersett (1875). 📢 🦅

Reconstruction Congress: focused entirely on African American male rights — women's property and legal rights treated as entirely separate question. No federal legislation. Coverture: married women still without independent legal identity in most states. Working-class women had fewest legal protections. 💭 💥
