heading: Gilded Age c.1877–1900
summary: The Gilded Age brought significant educational and employment gains — but suffrage stalled, pay remained half male wages, and Black and immigrant women were largely excluded from movement gains.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: No federal suffrage. State victories: Wyoming (1869), Colorado (1893), Utah (1896), Idaho (1896) — 4 states by 1900. NAWSA (1890): merger of NWSA and AWSA under Catt — 2 million members by 1919. National Association Opposed to Woman Suffrage (1911) organised anti-suffrage women. 📢

Minor v Happersett (1875) remained binding — blocked constitutional route. Women's political campaigns focused on 'moral' issues — temperance, poverty reform, settlement houses. Black women excluded from NAWSA's priorities. Ida B. Wells fought from outside mainstream movement. 📢 💥

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: No women in Congress or federal office. NAWSA and state campaigns building local political presence. Jeannette Rankin (first woman in Congress, 1916) still years away. Political influence channelled through reform organisations — WCTU, Hull House, NAWSA. 📢

State level: some women in school boards and local offices where allowed. But no women in state legislatures or governorships. Political parties refused to include women in leadership. Male political machines controlled nominations and appointments. 💭

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: WCTU under Frances Willard (from 1879): campaigned for temperance, women's suffrage and social reform — largest women's organisation of the era. Hull House (1889): Addams model of urban reform. National Consumer League (1899): workplace safety advocacy. Women's Crusade had demonstrated capacity for organised political pressure. 📢

No formal political influence. Temperance and reform organisations built women's public authority — but within 'moral' sphere. Male politicians listened to moral reform campaigns while ignoring suffrage demands. Black women entirely excluded from political influence. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Major gains: 111,000 women in higher education by 1870 (21% of all students) — 32% by 1880. By 1900 half of all high school graduates were female. c.1 million women employed as teachers, secretaries, librarians, telephone operators — clerical employment grew tenfold. 💰

BUT: education for middle-class women framed as preparation for marriage — not career. Working-class and immigrant women: no access to higher education. Black women excluded from most Southern educational institutions. Education gains concentrated among white, middle-class women. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Birth rate fell: 5.42 children per family (1850) → 3.56 (1900) — women gaining greater autonomy. Indoor plumbing, central heating, commercial laundries reduced domestic burdens. Hull House (1889): served 2,000 people per week by second year. WCTU established women's moral authority in public life. 📢 💰

Cult of domesticity remained dominant ideology. Black women excluded from mainstream women's movements. 1882 Lawrence strike received no support from male unions. Anti-suffrage organisations actively mobilised women against their own enfranchisement. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Comstock Laws (1873): federal criminalisation of contraceptive information — enforced throughout period. Birth rate decline suggested women finding informal means of reproductive control. No legal reproductive rights whatsoever. 🦅 💭

Social purity movement: moral reform around sexuality — often reinforced restrictions rather than challenging them. No public discussion of reproductive rights possible under Comstock Laws. Working-class and immigrant women most vulnerable to unwanted pregnancy — least able to access information. 💭

Comstock Laws (1873): federal law criminalising distribution of 'obscene' materials — including contraceptive information and abortion materials. Enforced aggressively — Sanger's first Brooklyn clinic shut down after serving 20,000 women. Remained in force for nearly 100 years. Legalisation of contraceptive information distribution to physicians — 1936 court ruling — first crack in Comstock framework. 🦅 💭

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Industrialisation: women in factories — textiles, garments, clerical. c.1 million in teaching, secretarial, clerical roles by 1900. BUT immigrant women: up to 70 hours per week for as little as $5. Women paid half male wages for equivalent work. No federal labour protections. 💰

By 1900 only 2% of trade unionists were women. AFL under Gompers excluded women workers. Black women confined to domestic service and sharecropping. Triangle Shirtwaist Factory conditions already entrenched — fire still 11 years away. No minimum wage, no safety standards, no maternity rights. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: KOL (1869): welcomed women, advocated equal pay. Women's Trade Union League (WTUL) founded 1903 — coalition for better wages and conditions. Bread and Roses Strike (1912): 20,000 immigrant women in Lawrence — won wage increases. 📢

AFL under Gompers excluded women — seen as undercutting male wages. 1882 Lawrence strike: no male union support. Only 2% of trade unionists were women by 1900. Working-class women's priorities (wages, safety) ignored by middle-class suffragists focused on the vote. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Legal coverture eroding slowly through state-level reforms — some married women gaining limited property rights. Married Women's Property Acts in some states gave limited independence. NAWSA lobbying for further state reforms. 🦅 📢

No federal legislation. No equal pay. No employment protections for women. Married women could still not access credit independently in most states. Black women faced double discrimination — race and sex excluded them from even limited legal gains. 💰 💥

obstacleKey: 🦅 Federal Government · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

heading: Progressive Era and WWI 1900–1920
summary: The Progressive Era and WWI produced the decisive breakthrough — the 19th Amendment (1920) — but also entrenched class and race divisions and produced significant labour gains alongside the vote.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: NAWSA: 2 million members by 1919 under Catt — combined state and federal strategy. CUWS (1913): Alice Paul — militant tactics, picketing White House, hunger strikes. Jeannette Rankin: first woman in Congress (1916, Montana). WWI: women's war service argument — 19th Amendment (1920) after 50 years of campaigning. 📢 ⚔️

But: only 1/3 of women voted in 1920s despite victory. Black women gained formal vote but faced voter suppression in South. At 1913 Suffrage Parade, NAWSA insisted Black women march at the back. 19th Amendment little thought given to Black women. ERA (1923): Alice Paul — rejected, regularly reintroduced. 📢 💥

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Jeannette Rankin: first woman in Congress (1916) — explicitly linked to war service and suffrage campaign. NAWSA and CUWS built networks of women political organisers. Some state legislatures gaining women members where suffrage had been granted. League of Women Voters (1920) followed. 📢

ERA rejected by Congress. Women remained marginal in federal government post-suffrage. Low voter turnout limited women's immediate political impact. Black women's political representation: essentially zero — voter suppression in South plus exclusion from white women's political organisations. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: WTUL influenced labour legislation. Sanger's birth control advocacy raised reproductive rights in public sphere. Women's moral authority used to push Progressive Era reforms — child labour, food safety, housing. Rankin in Congress voted against WWI entry — demonstrated women's distinctive political voice. 📢

WWI: women's war work used as suffrage argument — successfully. But male-dominated Progressive Era government slow to act on women's rights. FBI began monitoring activist women. Male politicians accepted women's war service while resisting political equality. ⚔️ 💭

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Women increasingly entering higher education. WTUL, settlement houses, women's colleges expanding training. Women entering teaching, nursing, social work as professions. WWI: women entered technical and professional training for war industries. 💰 ⚔️

Working-class and immigrant women: minimal access to formal education. School system reinforced gender roles — technical education closed to women. Black women: segregated institutions, HBCUs providing limited higher education. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Progressive Era: women as 'municipal housekeepers' — domestic expertise justified public reform role. Jane Addams, Ida B. Wells, Mother Jones: prominent female public figures. Sanger opened first birth control clinic (1916). WWI: 40% of women employed during war — surveys showed 40%+ wanted to continue. 📢 ⚔️

BUT: majority returned to domestic roles post-WWI. Red Scare: female independence framed as threatening. Temperance movement — 18th Amendment (1919) — showed women's moral authority but also reinforced middle-class moral impositions on working-class cultures. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Sanger: opened first birth control clinic (1916) despite Comstock Laws. American Birth Control League (1921): 222 clinics by 1941, later Planned Parenthood. Growing urban awareness of contraception. 📢

BUT: contraception illegal under Comstock Laws. Access limited to urban, wealthier women. Religious and conservative opposition intense. No legal reproductive rights progress. Working-class and rural women had least access — most vulnerable to unwanted pregnancy. 🦅 💭

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: WWI: women entered workforce in large numbers — industrial, clerical, professional. WTUL (1903): Lawrence Textile 'Bread and Roses' Strike (1912) — 20,000 workers won 15% pay rise and overtime. Women's Bureau in Department of Labor (1920): advocate for working women. 📢 ⚔️

Post-WWI: women pushed back into domestic roles. Wages remained substantially below male equivalent. No federal equal pay legislation. Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911): 146 killed — highlighted dangerous conditions and lack of union representation. 💭 💰

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: WTUL (1903): coalition of working-class and middle-class women — advocated for wages, hours, union membership. Lawrence Textile Strike (1912): IWW-led immigrant women — multicultural solidarity, 15% pay rise. Bryn Mawr Summer School for Women Workers (1921): labour rights education. 📢

AFL continued to exclude or marginalise women workers. Triangle Shirtwaist Fire exposed lack of protection. Class division: middle-class suffragists focused on vote; working-class women focused on wages and safety — priorities rarely aligned. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Progressive Era: some state-level property and legal reforms. Women entering legal and medical professions in small numbers. ERA (1923): Alice Paul — constitutional guarantee of equal rights proposed. Minor v Happersett overturned for voting by 19th Amendment — broader legal equality still absent. 📢 🦅

Coverture doctrine eroding through state reforms but no federal action. No maternity rights, no employment protection for pregnant women. Working women had no legal protection against sex discrimination. 💭

obstacleKey: 🦅 Federal Government · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

heading: 1920s–1932
summary: The 1920s brought the vote but limited political impact — flapper culture represented change for some while working-class, Black and immigrant women saw little improvement; Depression reversed employment gains.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: 19th Amendment (1920): vote granted — but only 1/3 of women voted in 1920s vs 2/3 of men. League of Women Voters (1920): educated women voters. Some women in state legislatures and federal Congress. Nellie Taylor Ross: first female governor (Wyoming, 1925–27). 📢

ERA (1923): rejected. Black women gained formal vote but faced voter suppression in South. No cohesive women's voting bloc emerged. Political parties slow to include women in leadership. Women's political influence weak — divided by class, race and party affiliation. 💥 🦅

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Growing number of women in state legislatures. Small number in Congress. Women's party caucuses developing. Some women in federal administrative positions. 📢

ERA rejected by Congress. Political machines controlled by men — women rarely selected for winnable seats. Black women's political representation: essentially zero. Anti-Suffrage League and conservative women actively opposed women in political leadership. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: League of Women Voters: civic education and political advocacy. Women's Bureau (1920): Department of Labor advocate for working women — limited enforcement powers. Shepherd-Towner Act (1921): first federal maternity and child health funding — women's lobbying success. 📢 🦅

Shepherd-Towner Act funding cancelled 1929 — showed fragility of women's political gains. ERA repeatedly rejected. Women's political organisations fragmented by class and race. Male-dominated party machines excluded women from real power. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Women's higher education growing — women 44% of undergraduates by 1930. Women entering professions — teaching, nursing, social work, some clerical and professional roles. Flapper culture partly product of educated, urban women asserting independence. 💰

BUT: college-educated women channelled toward 'feminised' lower-paid professions. Professional barriers to law, medicine, business remained strong. Working-class and immigrant women: no higher education access. Great Depression (1929): married women first to lose jobs — 'taking men's work'. 💭 💰

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Flapper culture: young, urban, middle-class white women — dancing, smoking, drinking, short hair, short skirts. Challenge to Victorian femininity. Birth rate continued to fall. Average marriage age rising. Cultural shift in urban middle-class context. 💰

BUT: flapper culture limited to white urban middle-class. Rural, working-class, Black and immigrant women unaffected. 80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll agreed married women should not take men's jobs. Many women maintained traditional roles. Contraception still illegal under Comstock Laws. 💭 💥

21st Amendment (1933): Prohibition repealed — marked waning influence of women-led temperance campaigns. WCTU had delivered the 18th Amendment (1919) as its greatest political victory; its repeal showed limits of moral reform as political strategy. Molly Pitcher Club (1922): women who opposed Prohibition argued against middle-class moral imposition on working-class communities. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: American Birth Control League (1921): Sanger expanded clinic network — 222 clinics by 1941. Growing urban access to contraception. Molly Pitcher Club (1922): women's opposition to Prohibition — challenged middle-class moral imposition. 📢

Comstock Laws still in federal force — federal prohibition on contraceptive information. Class divide: wealthier urban women had access, poor rural women did not. No legal reproductive rights. Abortion illegal in almost all circumstances. Religious and conservative opposition remained intense. 🦅 💭

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Women entering clerical and white-collar work in larger numbers — 1920s economic boom created opportunities. Women's Bureau (1920) advocated for working women. Some growing professional employment. 💰

BUT: Great Depression (1929): women first targeted for job losses — 'taking men's jobs'. Wages already half male equivalent. Married women under intense pressure to leave workforce. No minimum wage for women. Welfare Capitalism: some employer-provided benefits but excluded most women workers. 💭 💰

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: Women's union membership growing slowly. WTUL continued advocacy. Coalition of Labor Union Women developing. Some gains in textile unions. 📢

AFL under Gompers largely excluded women. Women concentrated in non-unionised sectors — domestic service, garment work, clerical. Great Depression devastated women workers — among first laid off. Union solidarity rarely extended to women. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Coverture doctrine continuing to erode — married women gaining more property and contract rights at state level. Women entering law profession in small numbers. ERA (1923) proposed federal constitutional equality — rejected. 🦅 📢

No federal equal pay, no maternity rights, no employment protection. Married women's independent legal identity weak in many states. Banks required husband's signature for loans and credit. Great Depression reinforced women's economic dependence on male breadwinners. 💭

obstacleKey: 🦅 Federal Government · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

heading: New Deal 1933–1941
summary: The New Deal brought the first female Cabinet member and some gains for women — but most programmes excluded or marginalised women, particularly women of colour, and reinforced the male breadwinner model.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: Frances Perkins: first female Cabinet member — Secretary of Labour 1933–45, influential in labour legislation. Mary McLeod Bethune: led National Youth Administration's Negro Affairs Division — part of 'Black Cabinet'. Florence Allen: first female U.S. Circuit Court judge. Nellie Taylor Ross: Director of U.S. Mint. 🦅 📢

ERA still rejected. Women remained marginal in Congress. Black women faced double discrimination. 80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll agreed married women should not take men's jobs. Male breadwinner assumption dominated all New Deal thinking. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Eleanor Roosevelt: transformed First Lady role — public advocate for civil rights and women's rights, advised FDR on appointments. Model of women's public leadership. Bethune in Black Cabinet showed women of colour could influence federal policy. 📢 🦅

But individual exceptions not systemic change. Few women in Congress. Black women faced race and sex discrimination simultaneously. Male-dominated Democratic Party machine controlled appointments. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Eleanor Roosevelt's influence pushed some inclusion of women in New Deal programmes. Women's organisations lobbied for Social Security, WPA, minimum wage. Frances Perkins directly shaped FLSA (1938) and Social Security Act (1935). 📢 🦅

But New Deal assumed male breadwinner as default throughout. CCC excluded women entirely. Aid to Dependent Children reinforced motherhood role over economic independence. Public opinion strongly opposed to married women working. 💭

subheadings.label: Education
facts: New Deal provided some adult education through WPA. Women's colleges continued to expand. By 1940 more women in higher education than ever. Some vocational training for women through relief programmes. 🦅 💰

CCC: completely excluded women. WPA limited women to 'appropriate' roles — domestic, clerical. Working-class and immigrant women: no educational opportunities from New Deal. Black women excluded from most programmes. New Deal reinforced gendered educational tracking. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Eleanor Roosevelt: model of women's public authority and advocacy. WTUL and women's organisations continued campaigning. Some radio broadcasts and publications normalising women's political commentary. 📢

80% in 1936 Gallup poll: married women should not work. New Deal reinforced male breadwinner model — Aid to Dependent Children assumed mother at home. CCC explicitly for men. WPA preferred male workers. Depression reinforced economic and cultural arguments for women's domestic role. 💭 💰

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: American Birth Control League: 222 clinics by 1941. Sanger's advocacy normalising birth control discussion in urban areas. Growing medical profession support for contraception. 📢

Comstock Laws still in force. No federal reproductive rights. Aid to Dependent Children (1935): supported single mothers but reinforced traditional motherhood role. Depression made unwanted pregnancy more economically devastating. 🦅 💭

1936 court ruling: legalised distribution of contraceptive information and materials to physicians — first significant break in Comstock Laws framework. American Birth Control League operating 222 clinics by 1941. Growing medical profession support for contraception. BUT: Comstock Laws still in force for general public — access remained deeply unequal. 📢

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: WPA employed 400,000 women by 1938. Social Security Act (1935): first federal safety net — some coverage for women. By 1940 800,000 women union members — 300% increase since 1930. Frances Perkins influenced labour legislation protecting workers generally. 🦅 📢

FLSA (1938): minimum wages but reinforced gender disparities — female teachers earned 20% less than male (1939). CCC excluded women entirely. WPA: one-family-member policy favoured men. Social Security excluded domestic and agricultural workers — majority women of colour. 🦅 💥

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: CIO (1935): more inclusive than AFL — welcomed women workers. By 1940 women's union membership 800,000 — 300% increase. Wagner Act (1935) enabled collective bargaining — benefited some women workers. 1937 Steelworkers' Strike: women played central organising roles. 📢 🦅

AFL still largely excluded women. Most New Deal labour programmes assumed male worker. Domestic and agricultural sectors — where most women of colour worked — excluded from labour protections entirely. Mexican American women vulnerable to deportation campaigns. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Social Security Act (1935): Aid to Dependent Children — first federal support for single mothers, though reinforced domestic role. FLSA (1938): minimum wage and maximum hours — some benefit for women workers. Eleanor Roosevelt's advocacy pushed for women's inclusion. 🦅

No maternity rights, no employment protection for pregnant women. Credit and banking required husband's co-signature. Black women excluded from New Deal relief locally administered in South by white officials. No constitutional equality. 💭 💥

obstacleKey: 🦅 Federal Government · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

heading: WWII and Post-War 1941–1963
summary: WWII transformed women's employment but the post-war retrenchment reinforced domesticity — Friedan's Feminine Mystique (1963) named the contradiction that would fuel new feminism.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: Women's political participation growing. Kennedy Commission on the Status of Women (1961): first federal acknowledgement of systematic discrimination — produced report confirming pervasive inequality. Some women in Congress — small but growing numbers. 🦅 📢

ERA still rejected. Black women continued to face voter suppression in South until VRA (1965). Women's political organisations focused on civic education not feminist demands. No cohesive women's political bloc until 1960s. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Wartime roles expanded women in federal government. Post-war: women's political participation remained low. Eisenhower era: no significant women's rights legislation. Kennedy Commission (1961): documented pervasive discrimination — set agenda for Equal Pay Act and Civil Rights Act. 🦅

ERA still rejected. Cold War conformity: women's role as homemaker/mother dominant political narrative. Male-dominated parties excluded women from leadership positions. Women's political ambitions suppressed by 1950s domestic ideal. 💭

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Kennedy Commission on Status of Women (1961): Esther Peterson led — first federal body documenting systematic sex discrimination. Influenced Equal Pay Act (1963) and Civil Rights Act Title VII (1964) — both just ahead. 🦅 📢

But: wartime gains rolled back by GI Bill male breadwinner model. Eisenhower era: women's rights not a federal priority. Cold War: domestic sphere as women's patriotic duty — framed as anti-communist family values. 🦅 💭

subheadings.label: Education
facts: WWII: women entered professional and technical training for war industries. Pill approved FDA (1960): revolutionary impact on women's life choices and education planning. By 1950 women 30% of undergraduates — below 1920s level due to GI Bill's male focus. 💰 ⚔️

GI Bill (1944): disproportionately benefited men — women veterans had less access to educational benefits. 1950s domestic ideal: education for women framed as preparation for housewifery. Dr Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946): 23 million copies — encouraged women to embrace nurturing role. 💭 🦅

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Rosie the Riveter: iconic WWII image — 6 million women entered workforce by 1944, 1 in 4 married women working outside home. 75% of women wanted to remain employed after WWII — distinct from post-WWI attitude. ⚔️ 💰

Post-war retrenchment: 2 million women lost jobs in 1946 as men returned. 1950s suburban housewife ideal dominant — Dr Spock, nuclear family, Cold War conformity. Friedan's Feminine Mystique (1963): named middle-class women's alienation from prescribed domestic role. 💭 💰

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Pill approved by FDA (1960): gave women control over reproductive health. Birth rate fell from 3.65 per woman (1960) to 1.86 (1976). Average marriage age rose from 20.3 (1960) to 23.3 (1980). Griswold v Connecticut (1965): Supreme Court struck down state contraceptive bans for married couples. 💰 🦅

But: Pill illegal for unmarried women until Eisenstadt v Baird (1972). Abortion illegal in almost all states. Comstock Laws still restricting information. Working-class and minority women had least access to Pill in early years. 🦅 💭

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: WWII: massive employment gains — 40% of women employed during war. Equal Pay Act (1963): first federal legislation on pay discrimination — women earning 59 cents per dollar earned by men. Women's Bureau continued advocacy throughout. 💰 ⚔️

GI Bill: male veterans received housing, education and job training — women veterans had far less access. Post-war: women pushed back to domestic roles, 2 million jobs lost 1946. Glass ceiling in management and professional positions entrenched. 💭 🦅

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: WWII: women's union membership grew — war industries highly unionised. Kennedy EO 10988 (1962): federal employees right to organise — included women. AFL-CIO merger (1955): 16 million members, some women included. 📢 ⚔️

Post-war: women pushed out of unionised industrial jobs as men returned. AFL-CIO leadership predominantly male. Women concentrated in non-unionised sectors — domestic service, clerical, retail. Gender discrimination in unions entrenched. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Coverture doctrine continuing to erode at state level. Kennedy Commission (1961): documented pervasive legal and economic discrimination — set agenda for reform. Some state-level family law reforms. 🦅

No federal equal pay until Equal Pay Act (1963). Credit discrimination: banks required husband's signature. No maternity protections. Property rights still limited for married women in many states. Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII still to come. 💭

obstacleKey: 🦅 Federal Government · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

heading: New Feminism 1963–1973
summary: The decade from 1963 to 1973 saw the most concentrated legislative and social gains for women — but the movement remained largely white and middle-class, and radical feminism provoked the backlash that followed.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: NOW (1966): founded by Friedan — radical feminist group advocating social, economic and cultural progress. National Women's Political Caucus (1971). ERA passed Congress (1972): sent to states for ratification after almost 50 years. Women's Strike for Equality (1970): nationwide demonstration. Ms Magazine (1972): Gloria Steinem — feminist political culture in mainstream. 📢

ERA required state ratification — Schlafly's Stop ERA campaign already organising. Black women's concerns still marginalised by predominantly white NOW. Jeannette Rankin Brigade (1968): women's anti-Vietnam War coalition. Women increasingly running for office but still dramatically underrepresented. 💥

VRA (1965): targeted poll taxes, literacy tests and discriminatory practices — enabled women of colour to exercise political rights suppressed since 19th Amendment (1920). Black women's voter registration in Mississippi: 6% (1964) → 60% (1969). VRA transformed the 19th Amendment from formal to real for Black women 45 years after its passage. 🦅

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Women increasingly winning federal and state offices. Betty Friedan and NOW raised profile of women's political under-representation as civil rights issue. Congressional Women's Caucus developing. Some gains in party leadership. 📢

ERA's failure — if it had passed — would have transformed political landscape. Male political establishment slow to concede leadership positions. Black women's specific political concerns marginalised by predominantly white mainstream feminist movement. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Equal Pay Act (1963): Kennedy Commission's recommendation implemented — first federal equal pay legislation. Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: sex discrimination prohibited — EEOC established. Title IX (1972): prohibited sex discrimination in federally funded education. Roe v Wade (1973): Supreme Court decision. NOW and feminist organisations central to all these. 📢 🦅

ERA passed Congress 1972 but state ratification campaign immediately contested. EEOC under-resourced to enforce Title VII. Roe immediately provoked National Right to Life Committee. Federal government gave with one hand (Title IX, Roe) while conservative movement organised to take back with another. 💥

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Title IX (1972): prohibited sex discrimination in federally funded education — transformative for women's access to higher education, sports, professional training. By 1970 nearly 40% of women enrolled in higher education vs 15% in 1950. Women entering law, medicine and other professions in growing numbers. 🦅 📢

Title IX implementation slow and contested — male sports establishment resisted. Professional glass ceiling remained. Black and working-class women had least access to expanding educational opportunities. Radical feminist critique: education system still structured around male norms. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Friedan's Feminine Mystique (1963): named middle-class women's alienation from domestic role — launched second-wave feminism. Miss America Protest (1968): rejection of objectification. Sexual revolution: Pill transformed sexual culture — women could delay marriage and control fertility. Divorce rate rising — women increasingly able to leave marriages. 📢 💰

Radical feminists: called for abolition of marriage, full societal overhaul. 'Radicalesbians' sparked backlash. Black Power influence: intersectionality — Angela Davis, Fannie Lou Hamer raised Black women's specific concerns. Radical feminism energised movement but also alienated moderates. 📢 💥

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Griswold v Connecticut (1965): contraception for married couples. Eisenstadt v Baird (1972): extended to unmarried individuals. National Organisation for Repeal of Abortion Laws (1969). Roe v Wade (1973): landmark federal judicial protection — right to abortion under constitutional privacy. 🦅 📢

Roe immediately polarising — National Right to Life Committee formed 1973. Hyde Amendment (1976) still ahead — would restrict federal abortion funding. Access remained unequal by class and race. Anti-abortion movement began organising immediately. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Equal Pay Act (1963): prohibited pay discrimination by sex. Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: prohibited employment discrimination by sex. Pregnancy Discrimination Act (1978) still ahead. Women in white-collar jobs growing. NOW fought workplace discrimination. CLUW (Coalition of Labor Union Women) founded 1974. 📢 🦅

Gender pay gap narrowing slowly — 59 cents (1963) → 71 cents (1973) per dollar. Glass ceiling intact. Progress mainly for white professional women — Black women and women of colour faced compounded barriers. Domestic workers and agricultural workers still excluded from key protections. 💥 💰

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: NOW advocacy pushed labour movement to address sex discrimination. Equal Pay Act and Title VII changed legal landscape for union negotiations. CLUW (1974): women's voice within AFL-CIO. Women's union membership growing through 1960s and 1970s — particularly in public sector (nurses, teachers). 📢

AFL-CIO leadership remained male-dominated. Private sector unions slow to incorporate women's concerns. Working-class and minority women's needs still secondary. Schlafly's Stop ERA campaign explicitly targeted working-class women — argued ERA would remove protections. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Title IX (1972): equal access in federally funded education. Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974): married women's right to credit in own name — banks previously required husband's signature. ERA passed Congress 1972 — would have enshrined constitutional equality. 📢 🦅

ERA still required state ratification — only 35 of 38 states by 1982 deadline. Pregnancy Discrimination Act (1978) still ahead. No constitutional guarantee of sex equality. Conservative legal movement mobilising against feminist legal gains. 💥

obstacleKey: 🦅 Federal Government · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

heading: Backlash Era 1973–1992
summary: The period from 1973 to 1992 saw the ERA defeated, abortion rights under sustained attack and Reagan's welfare cuts disproportionately harming women — but also significant economic, educational and political gains.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: ERA: only 35 of 38 states ratified by 1982 deadline — failed. Schlafly's Stop ERA: argued ERA would eliminate protections, force women into combat, destroy traditional family. Geraldine Ferraro: first woman nominated for VP (Democrats, 1984). 1992 'Year of the Woman': 24 women elected to House, 6 to Senate. 📢 💥

By 1992: women 11% of House, 5% of Senate — dramatically underrepresented. 55% of eligible women voted in 1992 vs 49% of men — women now more likely to vote. Sandra Day O'Connor: first woman on Supreme Court (1981). But ERA's failure meant no constitutional sex equality. 📢 🦅

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Growing numbers of women in state and federal offices. Congressional Women's Caucus active. Black women politicians: Barbara Jordan, Shirley Chisholm. Sandra Day O'Connor (1981): first female Supreme Court Justice. 'Year of the Woman' (1992) showed growing female electoral force. 📢

heading: 🔑 DS1.1 — How did the Gilded Age impact women's rights?
summary: The Gilded Age brought significant educational and workforce gains — but suffrage stalled, pay remained half male wages, and Black and immigrant women were largely excluded from movement gains.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: Gains
facts: Education: 111,000 women in higher education by 1870 (21%) — 32% by 1880. By 1900 half of all high school graduates were female. c.1 million employed as teachers, secretaries, librarians, telephone operators — clerical employment grew tenfold. Birth rate fell: 5.42 per family (1850) → 3.56 (1900). 💰

Domestic improvements: indoor plumbing, central heating, commercial laundries reduced household burdens. WCTU (1874) under Willard: campaigned for social reform, established women's moral authority in public life. Hull House (1889): served 2,000 per week. National Consumer League (1899). State suffrage victories: Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, Idaho. 📢

subheadings.label: Limitations
facts: No federal suffrage — Minor v Happersett (1875) confirmed citizenship did not guarantee vote. Only 4 states had female suffrage by 1900. Women paid half male wages — immigrant women worked 70 hours per week for $5. Only 2% of trade unionists were women by 1900. Black women excluded from mainstream suffrage movement. 💭 💥

Education for middle-class women framed as preparation for marriage — not career. Working-class and immigrant women had no access to higher education gains. Hull House and WCTU focused on middle-class white women's concerns. Comstock Laws (1873): criminalised contraceptive information. Birth control and reproductive rights taboo. 💭 🦅

heading: 🔑 DS1.2 — How effective were women's movements in the Gilded Age?
summary: Women's movements achieved significant social reform and some state suffrage victories but failed to win federal suffrage and remained divided along class and race lines.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: Effective
facts: NWSA: activist tactics — Anthony attempted to vote (1872), arrest and $100 fine she refused to pay. Garnered national attention. AWSA: state-by-state — Wyoming (1869), Colorado (1893), Utah (1896). NAWSA (1890): unified movement. WCTU under Willard: largest women's organisation, established moral authority in public life. Hull House: model of urban social reform. 📢

National Consumer League (1899): workplace advocacy. YWCA (1867): helped young women migrating to cities. Mother Jones: organised mine workers, led 1903 march of factory children. National Association of Coloured Women (1896): Ida B. Wells — fought for Black women's rights excluded from mainstream movements. 📢

National Consumer League (1899): Florence Kelley led — advocated for workplace safety and fair wages in industries dominated by women. Muller v Oregon (1908): NCL's brief helped establish state right to limit women's working hours. YWCA (established 1867): helped young single women migrating to cities find jobs and better living conditions. 📢

subheadings.label: Ineffective
facts: Male-dominated unions refused to support women's strikes — 1882 Lawrence strike received no union support. Only 2% of trade unionists women by 1900. Middle-class white women dominated movements — working-class, immigrant and Black women excluded or marginalised. NAWSA insisted Black women march at back of 1913 parade. 💥 💭

No federal suffrage achieved despite decades of campaigning. Minor v Happersett (1875) legally blocked constitutional route. ERA not proposed until 1923. Divisions between NWSA and AWSA weakened national campaign until NAWSA merger (1890). Women's movements focused on 'moral' sphere rather than fundamental legal change. 💥

obstacleKey: 🦅 Federal Government · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

heading: 🔑 DS1.3 — How united were women in the Gilded Age?
summary: Women showed some unity around suffrage and temperance — but were deeply divided by class, race and ideology in ways that significantly limited the movement's effectiveness.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: United
facts: NWSA and AWSA: despite tactical divisions both pushed for women's suffrage — united in goal if not method. NAWSA (1890): merger demonstrated capacity for unity. Higher education and workforce entry bridged some class gaps — both middle-class and working-class women benefiting from urbanisation. WCTU brought diverse women together around temperance. 📢

Settlement house movement: Hull House brought middle-class reformers into working-class communities — some cross-class solidarity. State suffrage victories required broad coalitions. Women's industrial leagues: some efforts at united action for wages and conditions. 📢 💰

subheadings.label: Disunited
facts: Class divisions: middle-class women focused on suffrage and temperance — working-class women focused on wages and labour rights. Temperance: middle-class imposition on working-class immigrant cultures that used alcohol as social practice. 1882 Lawrence strike received no suffragist support. Only 2% of trade unionists were women by 1900. 💥 💰

Race divisions: Black women excluded from NAWSA and mainstream suffrage organisations. Ida B. Wells: fought double oppression of racism and sexism from outside mainstream movement. National Association of Coloured Women (1896) — separate organisation required. NAWSA prioritised white Southern women's support over Black inclusion. 💥

heading: 🔑 DS2.1 — How strong was the position of women by 1932?
summary: By 1932 women had won the vote but made limited political use of it — gains in education and employment were real but the gender pay gap, union exclusion and reproductive restrictions persisted.

subheadings.label: Strengths
facts: 19th Amendment (1920): vote secured after 50 years. League of Women Voters: educated women voters. Women entering higher education in larger numbers — 44% of undergraduates by 1930. ERA introduced (1923) — showed ambition for constitutional equality. Nellie Taylor Ross: first female governor (Wyoming 1925). Women's Bureau (1920): advocate within federal government. 📢

Employment growth: women entering clerical and professional work — 1 million in teaching, secretarial, clerical roles. American Birth Control League: 222 clinics by 1941 expanding contraception access. WTUL advocated for working women. Flapper culture — cultural loosening of gender restrictions in urban areas. 📢 💰

subheadings.label: Weaknesses
facts: Only 1/3 of women voted in 1920s — low political engagement. Black women faced voter suppression in South. ERA rejected by Congress. Women earned half male wages. Only 2% of trade unionists women. No federal equal pay, no maternity rights, no reproductive rights. 💭 💥 🦅

Great Depression (1929): women first targeted for job losses. 80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working. Contraception still illegal under Comstock Laws. Working-class and Black women worst affected by Depression with no safety net. 💰 💭

heading: 🔑 DS2.2 — How far did the New Deal improve the position of women?
summary: The New Deal brought Frances Perkins as first female Cabinet member and some economic gains — but most programmes reinforced the male breadwinner model and excluded women of colour.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: Major Improvements
facts: Frances Perkins: first female Cabinet member — Secretary of Labour 1933–45, influential in labour legislation. Mary McLeod Bethune: Negro Affairs Division, part of Black Cabinet. Florence Allen: first female U.S. Circuit Court judge. WPA employed 400,000 women by 1938. By 1940 800,000 women union members — 300% increase since 1930. 🦅 📢

Social Security Act (1935): Aid to Dependent Children — first federal support for single mothers. FLSA (1938): minimum wages and maximum hours. Eleanor Roosevelt transformed First Lady role — public civil rights and women's rights advocate. CIO under Lewis more inclusive of women workers than AFL. 🦅

subheadings.label: Limited Gains
facts: FLSA (1938): set minimum wage but reinforced gender wage disparities — female teachers earned 20% less than male in 1939. CCC excluded women entirely. WPA: one-family-member policy favoured men. New Deal assumed male breadwinner as default. Social Security excluded domestic and agricultural workers — majority women of colour. 🦅 💥

80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working. Aid to Dependent Children reinforced motherhood role. Many relief programmes administered locally in South — Black women systematically excluded. Mexican American women vulnerable to deportation. Little thought given to working women's specific needs. 💭 💥

heading: 🔑 DS2.3 — How universal was the experience of women during the New Deal?
summary: New Deal programmes claimed to help all Americans but women had profoundly different experiences based on race, class and geography — with women of colour bearing the worst of its exclusions.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

subheadings.label: Universal Experiences
facts: All women faced societal attitudes reinforcing homemaker role — 80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working. All women excluded from higher-paying jobs or political decision-making regardless of race or class. FLSA (1938) and Social Security brought some universal — if unequal — coverage. Depression itself devastated all women economically. 💭

WPA employed women across racial lines — though in segregated and unequal conditions. Aid to Dependent Children reached single mothers across races — though unequally administered. Eleanor Roosevelt's advocacy raised women's profile generally. New Deal rhetoric of inclusion nominally applied to women. 🦅

subheadings.label: Very Different Experiences
facts: African American women: excluded from most relief programmes, domestic and agricultural work excluded from Social Security, CCC excluded women entirely. Urban Northern Black women had more access than rural Southern. Bethune's Black Cabinet role provided some influence — exceptional not typical. 💥 🦅

Mexican American women: domestic and agricultural work excluded from protections — vulnerable to deportation campaigns. Native American women: some benefit from IRA (1934) cultural preservation but excluded from mainstream New Deal networks. Urban white women: greater access to WPA, clerical jobs, union membership. Rural women — regardless of race: least access to all programmes. 💥 💰

heading: Black Power and Women's Rights 1965–1975
summary: The Black Power era had a complex relationship with women's rights — inspiring radical feminism while exposing deep divisions between mainstream and Black feminist movements.

subheadings.label: Advances
facts: Intersectionality: Black Power highlighted race, gender and class intersections — foundational concept for Black feminism. Angela Davis, Fannie Lou Hamer and Ella Baker gained national recognition.

Radical tactics: Black Power's direct action inspired second-wave feminism — Miss America protest (1968), CR consciousness-raising groups. NOW pressured EEOC on sex discrimination alongside racial discrimination.

subheadings.label: Limitations
facts: Male chauvinism within BPP: women relegated to secondary roles — 'Revolutionary first, Sister second.' NOI rejected birth control and challenged women in leadership.
Mainstream feminist movement (NOW) continued to focus on white middle-class issues — Black women's triple oppression (race, gender, class) not addressed until Third Wave feminism.

heading: 🔑 DS3.1 — How far did Black Power advance the position of Black women?
summary: Black Power raised the profile of Black women's triple oppression of race, gender and class — but male chauvinism within the movement meant women were simultaneously celebrated and subordinated.

subheadings.label: Gains
facts: Triple oppression recognised: race, gender and class intersection — foundational for Black feminism. Elaine Brown: Chairperson of Black Panther Party. Kathleen Cleaver: BPP spokesperson. Ericka Huggins: spearheaded free breakfast programmes. Women central to community engagement — day care, food programmes, health support. 📢

Angela Davis, Fannie Lou Hamer, Ella Baker: widely recognised figures. Malcolm X described Hamer as 'the country's number one freedom fighter'. Afro hairstyle: rejection of Eurocentric beauty standards — cultural reclamation for Black women. Women raised profile of Black women's specific concerns — education, healthcare, economic opportunity. 📢 💰

subheadings.label: Limitations
facts: Male chauvinism within BPP: women relegated to secondary roles — typing, cooking, logistics. Ideas proposed by women ignored unless proposed by men (Cleaver). Women expected to be 'revolutionary first, Sister second'. Angela Davis criticised for performing a 'man's job'. Women tasked with cooking and serving at meetings while men discussed strategy. 💭

NOI: rejected birth control, criticised women challenging traditional gender roles. Black Power leaders viewed feminism as 'white women's issue'. Focus on reclaiming Black masculinity limited gender equality within movement. Mainstream feminism (NOW) slow to incorporate Black women's concerns. 💥 💭

heading: 🔑 DS3.2 — How did Black Power influence the wider women's movement?
summary: Black Power's influence was significant — introducing intersectionality and radicalising tactics — but mainstream feminism continued to focus on white middle-class concerns.

subheadings.label: Major Influence
facts: Intersectionality: Black Power highlighted race, gender and class intersections — foundational concept for Black feminism and later mainstream feminist theory. Militant tactics: radical feminism in late 1960s and early 1970s adopted more direct-action approaches inspired by Black Panthers' emphasis on action over words. 📢

Angela Davis, Elaine Brown, Kathleen Cleaver: brought revolutionary spirit to feminism — demonstrated Black women could lead their own struggles. NOW pushed — slowly — to incorporate racial justice. Black women's activism raised profile of healthcare, education and economic opportunity as feminist concerns. 📢

Many white feminists slow to engage with racial justice. Radical feminist groups of 1970s often criticised as predominantly white and middle-class. 💥 💭

heading: The Role of Women's Campaigns
summary: Women's campaigns were the primary driver of rights gains — from the suffrage movement through to NOW and radical feminism — but consistently divided along class, race and ideological lines.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💥 Division

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: NWSA (1869): Anthony and Stanton — federal amendment strategy. AWSA (1869): Stone — state-by-state. Anthony arrested attempting to vote (1872). NAWSA (1890): merger, 2 million members by 1919. CUWS (1913): Alice Paul — militant tactics, picketing White House, hunger strikes. 19th Amendment (1920): 50-year campaign. 📢

State campaigns: Wyoming (1869), Colorado (1893), Utah (1896), Idaho (1896). ERA: Alice Paul (1923) — rejected, passed Congress 1972, failed ratification 1982. NOW (1966): Friedan — broader political and legal equality. National Women's Political Caucus (1971). Women's Strike for Equality (1970). ERA's failure showed limits of campaigns without constitutional backing. 📢

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Jeannette Rankin: first woman in Congress (1916). NAWSA and NOW lobbied for women candidates. League of Women Voters (1920): educated women voters. 'Year of the Woman' (1992): 24 women elected to House. ERA campaign raised constitutional equality as political issue for 60 years. 📢

Only 11% of House by 1992 despite decades of campaigning. ERA failed. Black women's political campaigns received little mainstream women's movement support. Schlafly successfully mobilised working-class women against ERA by arguing it would remove protections. 📢 💥

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: WCTU: 18th Amendment (1919) — demonstrated women's political influence before suffrage. WTUL: influenced labour legislation. NOW: lobbied for Title IX (1972), Civil Rights Act sex discrimination clause, Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974). Friedan and NOW pushed Kennedy to establish Commission on the Status of Women (1961). 📢

Radical feminism influenced cultural and policy shifts — Miss America protest (1968), Roe v Wade activism. CLUW (1974): women's voice within AFL-CIO. Mainstream campaigns often excluded working-class and Black women's concerns — limiting breadth of political influence. 📢 💥

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Hull House (1889): served 2,000 per week — education for poor immigrant women. YWCA (1867): jobs and education for urban women. NOW campaigned for Title IX (1972) — transformed women's educational access. Bryn Mawr Summer School for Women Workers (1921). 📢

WCTU and suffrage organisations built female leadership networks. But campaigns focused on middle-class women's needs — working-class and minority women's educational access rarely prioritised. Title IX implementation contested — required ongoing legal campaigning throughout 1970s–80s. 💥

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Friedan's Feminine Mystique (1963): named 'the problem with no name' — launched second-wave feminism. Miss America protest (1968): symbolic rejection of objectification. Ms Magazine (1972): feminist cultural politics in mainstream. Sanger's birth control advocacy: normalised discussion of reproductive health. 📢

WCTU: temperance as moral reform — established women's public authority but also imposed middle-class values. Radical feminism provoked significant backlash — Schlafly's movement a direct response. Cultural campaigns more effective when linked to concrete legal demands. 📢 💥

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Sanger: opened first birth control clinic (1916) despite Comstock Laws. American Birth Control League (1921) — 222 clinics by 1941, later Planned Parenthood. National Organisation for Repeal of Abortion Laws (1969). NOW central to Roe v Wade (1973) campaign. Griswold (1965) campaign achieved contraceptive rights. 📢

Hyde Amendment (1976): campaigns failed to prevent federal funding restriction. Anti-abortion movement organised immediately after Roe. Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992): ongoing vulnerability without ERA protection. Access remained unequal by class and race despite legal victories. 📢 💥

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: WTUL (1903): organised working women — Lawrence Textile Strike (1912), 15% pay rise. NOW lobbied for Equal Pay Act (1963) and Title VII sex discrimination clause. CLUW (1974): women within AFL-CIO. NOW advocacy throughout 1970s–80s on workplace equality. 📢

Gender pay gap narrowed slowly — 59 cents (1963) to 75 cents (1992) per dollar. Glass ceiling persisted. CLUW had limited impact on AFL-CIO male leadership. Working-class women's concerns — wages, safety — often secondary to middle-class campaigns for professional equality. 💥 💰

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: WTUL (1903): first sustained effort to organise women workers — Lawrence Strike (1912) landmark. KOL (1869) had earlier welcomed women. CLUW (1974) pushed AFL-CIO to address women's concerns. Bread and Roses strike (1912): multicultural solidarity demonstrated. 📢

Male union dominance: AFL excluded women throughout. By 1900 only 2% of trade unionists women. AFL-CIO leadership still male-dominated by 1992. Mainstream suffrage and labour campaigns rarely aligned — class and race divisions hindered united worker-feminist action. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: ERA: Alice Paul (1923) — proposed constitutional guarantee, reintroduced every Congress, passed 1972, failed ratification 1982. NOW legal campaigns: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974), Pregnancy Discrimination Act (1978). Title IX litigation. 📢

ERA failure was the defining limit of legal campaigns. Without constitutional backing every legislative gain was vulnerable. Schlafly's campaign showed conservative women's campaigns could be as effective as progressive ones. By 1992 fundamental legal equality not constitutionally enshrined. 💥

heading: The Role of the Federal Government
summary: The Federal Government was a crucial but inconsistent ally — the 19th Amendment, Title VII and Roe v Wade were transformative — but Comstock Laws, the ERA's failure and welfare cuts showed its limitations.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💥 Division

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: 19th Amendment (1920): 50 years after women first organised for suffrage. VRA (1965): extended effective voting rights to Black women suppressed in the South. ERA passed Congress (1972): sent to states — showed federal legislative willingness. Kennedy Commission on the Status of Women (1961): first federal acknowledgement of systematic discrimination. 🦅

15th Amendment (1870) explicitly excluded women. Minor v Happersett (1875): Supreme Court blocked constitutional route. No federal action between 1870 and 1920. ERA passed Congress but failed state ratification — federal government could not deliver constitutional equality. VRA only partially overcame suppression of Black women's vote. 🦅 💥

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Frances Perkins (1933): first female Cabinet member. Florence Allen: first female Circuit Court judge. Sandra Day O'Connor: first female Supreme Court Justice (1981). Geraldine Ferraro: first female VP nominee (1984). Jimmy Carter: appointed more women to federal judiciary than any previous president. 🦅

Federal government slow to appoint women. By 1992 women still only 11% of House and 5% of Senate despite 70+ years of suffrage. ERA's failure meant no constitutional bar to political exclusion. Reagan era reversed some appointments progress. Male-dominated executive branch throughout. 🦅 💭

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Eleanor Roosevelt: transformed First Lady role — advocated for civil rights and women's rights, influenced FDR appointments. Bethune in Black Cabinet. Kennedy Commission (1961): documented pervasive discrimination — set legislative agenda for Equal Pay Act. LBJ's Great Society: Head Start — benefited working women and mothers. 🦅

Federal government slow to act without sustained campaign pressure. Long periods of federal disinterest — 1877–1933, Reagan era rollback. Welfare cuts (Reagan 1980s) disproportionately harmed women. FBI surveilled feminist organisations similar to treatment of civil rights organisations. 🦅 💰

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Title IX (1972): prohibited sex discrimination in federally funded education — transformative for higher education access and sports. Some women veterans accessed GI Bill educational benefits. Freedmen's Bureau had established some precedent for federal education investment. 🦅

Federal government enforced Title IX slowly and reluctantly. Reagan era weakened Title IX enforcement. GI Bill explicitly favoured men. New Deal programmes (CCC) excluded women from education and training. Federal education policy long assumed male student as default. 🦅 💭

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Prohibition (18th Amendment 1919): demonstrated federal response to women's moral reform campaigns. Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: acknowledged gender discrimination as civil rights issue. Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974): federal recognition of credit discrimination against women. 🦅

Federal government often reinforced traditional gender roles — GI Bill assumed male breadwinner model. Reagan era 'traditional values' rhetoric reinforced anti-feminist attitudes. New Deal Aid to Dependent Children reinforced motherhood role over economic independence. 🦅 💭

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Griswold v Connecticut (1965): Supreme Court struck down state contraceptive bans — federal judicial protection of reproductive privacy. Eisenstadt v Baird (1972): extended to unmarried individuals. Roe v Wade (1973): landmark federal judicial protection of abortion rights. 🦅 📢

Comstock Laws (1873): federal criminalisation of contraceptive information for nearly 100 years. Hyde Amendment (1976): Congress restricted abortion funding — low-income women most affected. Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992): federal Supreme Court allowed state restrictions. ERA's failure meant no constitutional reproductive rights guarantee. 🦅 💥

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Equal Pay Act (1963): first federal legislation prohibiting pay discrimination by sex. Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: prohibited employment discrimination by sex — EEOC established. Pregnancy Discrimination Act (1978): banned discrimination based on pregnancy. Lanham Act (1941): funded childcare for war industry women. 🦅

New Deal excluded domestic and agricultural workers (most women of colour) from FLSA and Social Security. GI Bill favoured male veterans. Reagan welfare cuts and anti-union stance disproportionately harmed women workers. Women earning 75 cents per dollar by 1992 despite nearly 30 years of legislation. 🦅 💰

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: Wagner Act (1935): legalised collective bargaining — benefited women workers in unionised sectors. FLSA (1938): minimum wage and maximum hours. Kennedy EO 10988 (1962): federal employees right to organise. Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: prohibited union discrimination by sex. 🦅

Federal government long complicit in excluding women from labour protections. New Deal Social Security and labour laws excluded domestic and agricultural workers — most women of colour. Reagan's PATCO (1981): weakened unions generally — disproportionately affected women. 🦅 💥

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: ERA passed Congress (1972): sent to states — federal legislative commitment to constitutional equality. Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974): married women's right to independent credit. Pregnancy Discrimination Act (1978). Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII. Title IX (1972). 🦅

ERA failed ratification — federal government could not deliver constitutional sex equality. Supreme Court increasingly conservative post-Reagan appointments. Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992) allowed state abortion restrictions. By 1992 fundamental legal equality not constitutionally guaranteed. 🦅 💥

heading: The Role of War and Changing Employment
summary: War was the most powerful catalyst for women's employment gains — but each war was followed by retrenchment, and only WWII produced lasting attitudinal change toward women working.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💥 Division

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: Civil War: women's wartime service built case for political inclusion. WWI: women's war service explicitly linked to suffrage argument by NAWSA — contributed to 19th Amendment (1920). Women's wartime contribution made exclusion from democratic rights untenable. ⚔️

Civil War produced 15th Amendment excluding women — suffragists felt betrayed. WWI suffragists used militant tactics alongside war service argument. WWII service did not produce equivalent breakthrough — vote already gained. Cold War: domestic role emphasised as part of anti-communist family values. ⚔️ 💭

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: WWI: Jeannette Rankin elected to Congress (1916) — linked to women's war service and suffrage campaign. WWII: women's wartime roles built confidence for political participation. Post-WWII generation entered politics in larger numbers than before. ⚔️

Post-WWI retrenchment pushed most women back to domestic sphere. 1950s domestic ideal reduced women's political ambition. Cold War conformity: women's political role as homemaker supporters of family values. ⚔️ 💭

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: WWII: wartime necessity forced federal engagement with working women — Lanham Act (1941) funded childcare, Rosie the Riveter propaganda. Women's war service built moral claim for federal government to act on women's rights. ⚔️

Post-WWII: GI Bill (1944) reinforced male breadwinner — women's wartime gains rolled back. Cold War: domestic sphere as women's patriotic duty. Wartime gains proved temporary without legislative consolidation. ⚔️ 🦅

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Civil War: women nurses, teachers, administrators — proved women capable in professional roles. WWI: women entered technical and professional training. WWII: 6 million women entered workforce including professional and technical roles. War proved women's capability in roles previously reserved for men. ⚔️

Post-WWII: 1950s domestic ideal reduced women in higher education — from 40% (1920) to 30% (1950) of undergraduates. GI Bill educated male veterans not women. Vietnam era: military expanded educational opportunities for men not women. ⚔️ 💭

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Civil War: women's capabilities beyond domestic sphere recognised. WWI: 40% of women employed during war. WWII: most transformative — Rosie the Riveter iconography — 75% of women wanted to remain employed after war, distinct from post-WWI attitude. ⚔️

Post-WWI: majority returned to domestic roles — Red Scare framed female independence as threatening. Post-WWII: 1950s domestic ideal and Dr Spock rolled back WWII cultural shift. Vietnam War era: anti-war movement energised women politically — contributed to new feminism. ⚔️ 💭

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: WWII: women's workforce entry made reproductive control more practically necessary — Pill development driven partly by wartime social changes. Lanham Act (1941): federal childcare funding — temporary recognition working mothers needed support. ⚔️

Vietnam War era: feminist movement energised partly by anti-war activism — Roe v Wade (1973) followed. Wartime tends to reinforce traditional gender roles — women as mothers waiting at home. Post-war retrenchments repeatedly set back reproductive rights progress. ⚔️ 💭

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Civil War: 400,000+ war widows entered labour market through necessity. WWI: women's employment rate reached 40%. WWII: 6 million women entered workforce — by 1944 1 in 4 married women working outside home. 75% wanted to remain employed after WWII. ⚔️

Post-war retrenchment: 2 million women lost jobs in 1946 as men returned. GI Bill privileged male veterans — women not given equivalent education and job training. Women's wartime gains proved temporary without legal consolidation. Each war: advance then rollback. ⚔️ 💭 🦅

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: WWI and WWII: women entered unionised industrial sectors for first time at scale. Wartime labour solidarity created some cross-gender union experience. WTUL used wartime context to advance women's labour rights agenda. ⚔️

Post-war: women pushed out of unionised industrial jobs as men returned. Male unions actively excluded women from occupational territories — AFL patterns reinforced post-war. Women returned to non-unionised sectors. Each war followed by restoration of male union monopoly. ⚔️ 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Civil War widowhood: 400,000+ women had to manage property and finances independently — demonstrated capacity for legal and economic autonomy. Wartime service built general case for women's legal equality. WWII women's workforce entry began eroding coverture doctrine in practice. ⚔️

GI Bill (1944): reinforced male breadwinner as legal and economic norm — women as dependents. Post-war domestic ideal reinforced women's economic dependence. Wartime gains in legal autonomy largely reversed post-war. Legal framework lagged far behind women's demonstrated wartime capabilities. ⚔️ 💭

heading: The Role of Socioeconomic Change
summary: Industrialisation, urbanisation and economic development created new opportunities for women — but also new forms of exploitation — and the gender pay gap persisted from 1865 through to 1992.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💥 Division

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: Industrialisation: urbanisation concentrated women — collective action and political organisation became possible. Education gains created politically aware female population. By 1992 55% of women voted — more than men — product of long economic and educational development. 💰

Great Depression reinforced economic dependence that made political independence harder. Only 1/3 of women voted in 1920s despite having the vote — economic dependence shaped political behaviour. Working-class women prioritised wages over suffrage throughout Gilded Age and Progressive Era. 💥 💰

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Education gains drove political participation. Growing female professional class — lawyers, doctors, teachers — provided political leadership. Economic independence from 1960s enabled women to run for office. By 1992 women 11% of House — product of decades of educational and economic development. 💰

Economic inequality meant women remained financially dependent on men — limited political independence. Working-class women had least political representation in women's movements. Black women faced economic barriers compounding political exclusion. 💥 💰

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Industrial economy: women's consumer role gave moral authority over economic regulation — Progressive Era women as 'municipal housekeepers'. New Deal: Depression created opening for government intervention that women's organisations shaped. Great Society responded to women's advocacy around poverty and single motherhood. 💰 📢

Reaganomics: deindustrialisation and deregulation eroded the economic base for welfare state that most supported women. Gender pay gap persistence meant women had less economic and therefore political leverage throughout period. 💰 💭

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Industrialisation: economic demand for literate workers opened educational opportunities. By 1880 32% of higher education students were women. Clerical economy created demand for educated female workforce. By 1992 women outpaced men in high school graduation and approaching parity in higher education. 💰

Economic structure channelled educated women into 'feminised' lower-paid professions — teaching, nursing, secretarial. Working-class women had least access to educational gains. Great Depression: married women first to lose jobs including educated women. Glass ceiling persisted despite educational gains. 💰 💭

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Industrial economy: reduced household labour burden — plumbing, central heating, commercial laundries freed women's time. Birth rate decline (5.42 per family 1850 → 2.2 by 1992) — economic forces shaped family size decisions. Flapper culture: product of 1920s economic prosperity and urban independence. Pill (1960): combined with economic independence — transformed women's life choices. 💰

Each economic downturn reversed cultural gains — Depression reinforced domesticity, post-WWII prosperity promoted suburban housewife ideal. Economic dependence on male income maintained traditional gender attitudes well into 20th century. 80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working. 💭 💰

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Industrialisation: economic pressure to limit family size — birth rate already falling before contraception was legal. Pill (1960): economic and social context made reproductive control practically important for working women. Economic independence from 1960s made reproductive choice meaningful. 💰

Comstock Laws suppressed reproductive information regardless of economic need. Working-class and poor women had least access to Pill in early years — most needed reproductive control, least able to obtain it. Hyde Amendment (1976): low-income women most affected — economic penalty for reproductive choice. 💰 🦅

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Industrialisation opened factory and clerical work — by 1900 c.1 million women employed as teachers, secretaries, librarians. Clerical economy created mass female employment. By 1992 women 40% of workforce. Equal Pay Act (1963) and Title VII drove wage gains. 💰

Gender pay gap persistent: 1870 (50 cents per dollar) → 1963 (59 cents) → 1992 (75 cents). Slow progress despite legal framework. Women concentrated in lower-paid feminised sectors throughout period. Glass ceiling: women only 10% of management by 1992. Women of colour earned least. 💰 💭

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: Industrialisation created factory work for women — first large-scale female wage labour. KOL (1869): most inclusive early union, welcomed women. WTUL (1903). Lawrence Textile Strike (1912): immigrant women's economic power demonstrated. Bread and Roses: economic dignity as well as wages. 💰 📢

AFL excluded women — skilled male workers saw women as wage competition. By 1900 only 2% of trade unionists women. Deindustrialisation (1970s–80s): eliminated unionised manufacturing jobs where women had made most gains. Service sector expansion: lower wages, less unionised. 💰 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Industrialisation: women earning wages challenged coverture doctrine in practice — married women lobbied for property rights. Rising middle-class women's economic participation drove state-level property reforms from 1870s. Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974): product of women's growing economic role requiring independent credit. 💰

Depression (1929): rolled back women's economic independence — reinforced legal and economic dependence. By 1992 persistent gender wealth gap — consequence of lifetime of lower wages, interrupted careers, lower pension contributions. ERA's failure meant no constitutional economic equality guarantee. 💰 💥
