heading: Federal Government
summary: The Federal Government was a major obstacle — from Comstock Laws through to the ERA's failure and abortion restrictions — reflecting male-dominated political institutions' resistance to gender equality.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💥 Division

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: 15th Amendment (1870): explicitly excluded women — federal government granted vote to Black men not women. Minor v Happersett (1875): Supreme Court ruled citizenship did not guarantee voting rights. 50-year gap between 15th and 19th Amendments. Black women gained formal vote in 1920 but federal failure to enforce against Southern suppression. 🦅

ERA (1923–1982): Congress refused ERA until 1972 — then failed to ensure state ratification. By 1992 ERA still unratified — fundamental federal failure to constitutionally guarantee sex equality. Federal government never provided equivalent constitutional protection for sex as for race (14th/15th Amendments). 🦅

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Male-dominated Congress and executive branch consistently failed to prioritise women's rights legislation. Federal government slow to appoint women — long periods with virtually no women in senior federal roles. ERA's failure reflected legislature's unwillingness to guarantee constitutional equality. 🦅 💭

Reagan appointments to federal judiciary and Supreme Court: reversed some progress. Male-dominated judiciary consistently interpreted laws narrowly regarding sex discrimination until feminist litigation forced change from 1960s. 🦅

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Male-dominated Congress defeated ERA for decades. FBI under Hoover surveilled feminist organisations. Reagan administration explicitly hostile to feminist agenda — opposed ERA enforcement, Title IX, abortion rights. Federal government's male breadwinner assumption pervaded all legislation throughout. 🦅 💭

Federal government treated women's rights as special interest not fundamental right. Long gap between women winning vote (1920) and federal government taking gender equality seriously (1960s). Political establishment consistently slow and resistant without overwhelming campaign pressure. 🦅

subheadings.label: Education
facts: CCC excluded women entirely. GI Bill (1944) primarily benefited men — educational benefits not equally available to women veterans. Federal education policy assumed male student as norm throughout Gilded Age and Progressive Era. New Deal reinforced gender-segregated educational tracking. 🦅 💭

Title IX (1972) showed what federal action could achieve — but enforcement contested and slow. Reagan era weakened Title IX implementation. Women channelled into 'feminised' professions by federally supported educational structures. 🦅

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Comstock Laws (1873): federal legislation criminalised contraceptive information — active suppression of reproductive knowledge for nearly a century. New Deal Aid to Dependent Children reinforced motherhood role rather than economic independence. GI Bill celebrated male breadwinner as American ideal. 🦅 💭

Reagan era 'traditional values' rhetoric from federal executive reinforced anti-feminist attitudes. 1950s Cold War family values promoted at federal level. Federal government used cultural power to reinforce gender hierarchy throughout period. 🦅

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Comstock Laws (1873): federal law criminalising contraceptive information — enforced for nearly 100 years. Hyde Amendment (1976): federal Congress restricted abortion funding — low-income women most affected. ERA failure: no constitutional reproductive rights guarantee. 🦅

Supreme Court (federal judiciary): Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992) allowed state abortion restrictions — federal judicial backsliding. Reagan and Bush appointments to Supreme Court deliberately targeted at reversing Roe. Federal government long and consistently obstructed reproductive autonomy. 🦅 💥

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Federal government excluded women from labour protections: Social Security and FLSA excluded domestic and agricultural workers — majority women of colour. CCC excluded women. New Deal assumed male breadwinner. GI Bill disadvantaged women veterans. No federal equal pay until 1963. 🦅

Reagan welfare cuts and PATCO (1981) anti-union stance disproportionately harmed women workers. EEOC under-resourced to enforce Title VII sex discrimination. Women still earning 75 cents per dollar by 1992 despite nearly 30 years of legislation. 🦅 💰

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: Federal government consistently sided with employers against unions — disproportionately harmed women in unionised sectors. New Deal labour laws excluded most women workers. Reagan's PATCO (1981) assault on unions weakened collective bargaining affecting women in public and private sectors. 🦅

Government's right-to-work policies concentrated in South and West where women's wages lowest. Federal government never legislated equal representation of women in union leadership. Taft-Hartley (1947) anti-communist provisions hit CIO — more inclusive of women than AFL — hardest. 🦅 💥

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Federal government maintained coverture doctrine through inaction — no federal legislation protecting married women's property rights until well into 20th century. ERA passed Congress 1972 but federal government unable to ensure ratification — by 1992 no constitutional sex equality. 🦅 💥

Supreme Court long interpreted 14th Amendment narrowly to exclude sex discrimination claims. Reagan and Bush Supreme Court appointments deliberately targeted at conservative interpretation of sex equality. Federal judiciary as obstacle as well as enabler. 🦅

obstacleKey: 🦅 Federal Government · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition

heading: Attitudes in Society
summary: Attitudes in society — male institutional power, female conservatism, religious ideology and cultural norms — were the most pervasive and persistent obstacle to women’s rights across the entire period, operating from within the home as much as from outside it.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: Anti-suffrage male politicians: decades of congressional rejection. Anti-Suffrage League: argued women's primary role was in the home, involvement in politics would cause disorder. Male opposition to suffrage framed as protecting women — paternalistic and controlling. Minor v Happersett (1875) decided by all-male judiciary. 💭

Post-suffrage: male politicians and parties slow to take women's political priorities seriously. ERA opposed by male-dominated Congress for decades. 80% of Americans (1936 Gallup): married women should not take men's jobs. Nixon and Reagan: coded appeals to male resentment of feminist gains. 💭

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Male-dominated Congress: consistently marginalised women's concerns and delayed women's rights legislation. Party systems controlled by men — women token inclusions not structural partners. Male party bosses determined candidate selection — women consistently overlooked for safe seats. 💭

Black Power: male chauvinism — women expected to be 'revolutionary first, Sister second'. Trade union male leadership excluded women from negotiating table and union leadership positions throughout period. Male politicians listened to moral reform campaigns while ignoring structural equality demands. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Male-dominated governments: women's campaigns required extraordinary effort to even be heard. Male politicians dismissed suffragists, ERA advocates, reproductive rights campaigners as special interests. FBI under Hoover surveilled women's organisations. 💭 🦅

Schlafly's Stop ERA campaign empowered by male conservative political establishment. Evangelical Christian male leadership provided institutional base for anti-feminist backlash. Male union leaders actively excluded women from labour movement leadership and bargaining tables throughout period. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Male academics and institutions excluded women from higher education — only 3% of women in college by 1870. Professional training (law, medicine, business) closed to women by male-dominated institutions. Educational curriculum designed around male experience — women's achievements systematically excluded. 💭

Post-WWII: male-defined ideal of educated housewife — college for women as preparation for marriage. Dr Spock's 23-million-copy bestseller promoted male breadwinner/female nurturer model. Title IX (1972) contested by male sports establishment — decades of litigation to enforce. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Cult of domesticity: dominant male-constructed ideology — women as moral guardians of home, subordinate to male breadwinner. Social Darwinism and religious ideology provided intellectual and spiritual justification for gender hierarchy. Male-controlled media stereotyped and objectified women throughout period. 💭

Schlafly's Stop ERA campaign articulated male conservative establishment's response to feminist challenge. Evangelical Christianity resurgence (1970s–80s): male religious authority reasserted. Anti-abortion movement: predominantly male leadership asserting control over women's bodies. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Comstock Laws (1873): passed by male-dominated Congress — criminalised contraceptive information. Male medical establishment controlled access to contraception and abortion. 'Backstreet abortion' killed thousands — male-controlled legal system maintained criminalisation. 💭 🦅

Anti-abortion movement post-Roe: predominantly male evangelical and Catholic leadership. Reagan and Bush male-dominated administrations made opposing abortion a political priority. Hyde Amendment: male-dominated Congress restricted federal abortion funding directly targeting low-income women. 💭 🦅

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Wage discrimination: male employers paid women half male wages from Gilded Age to 1992 — 59 cents (1963) → 75 cents (1992) per dollar. Glass ceiling: male management excluded women from senior positions — only 10% of management by 1992. Male-dominated professions actively resisted female entry. 💭

Male union exclusion: AFL under Gompers explicitly excluded women — seen as wage competition. Only 2% of trade unionists women by 1900. Post-WWII: male unions active in pushing women out of industrial jobs. 80% public opinion (1936) supported excluding married women from workforce. 💭 💥

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: AFL exclusion: Gompers and male union leadership explicitly excluded women. Even inclusive unions (KOL) failed to maintain women's inclusion long-term. Male union leadership throughout period marginalised women's concerns. 💭 💥

Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911): male factory owners locked exit doors — killed 146 women workers. Male union leaders failed to represent women in negotiations. AFL-CIO male leadership: women remained marginal despite CLUW's efforts from 1974. 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: Coverture doctrine: built on male supremacy — women's legal identity subsumed by husband at marriage. Designed, maintained and interpreted by male-dominated legal profession and judiciary. Married women could not own property, sign contracts or keep wages — enforced by male courts. 💭 🦅

Male-dominated legal profession slow to challenge discriminatory laws. Minor v Happersett (1875): all-male Supreme Court. ERA opposed by male political establishment. Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992): conservative male-appointed Supreme Court allowed state abortion restrictions. 💭 🦅

heading: Division and Conservative Opposition
summary: Division within the women's movement — by class, race, ideology and marital status — combined with organised conservative opposition to create a significant internal and external obstacle throughout the period.
factorKey: 📢 Women's Campaigns · 🦅 Federal Government · ⚔️ War · 💰 Socioeconomic Change · 💥 Division

subheadings.label: The Vote
facts: NWSA vs AWSA (1869): split over 15th Amendment and strategy — weakened suffrage campaign for 20 years until NAWSA merger (1890). CUWS vs NAWSA: militant vs moderate tactics from 1913. ERA battle: NOW vs Schlafly's Stop ERA — conservative women as active opponents of women's rights. 📢 💥

Race divisions: NAWSA excluded Black women — insisted they march at back of 1913 parade. 19th Amendment secured for white women — Black women faced voter suppression. Black women had to fight on two fronts simultaneously. Anti-Suffrage League: organised women actively opposing their own enfranchisement. 💥

subheadings.label: Political Representation
facts: Class divisions: middle-class women focused on suffrage — working-class women focused on wages and labour rights. These rarely aligned. Temperance: middle-class imposition on working-class immigrant cultures — created resentment. Different feminist organisations competed for same political space. 💥 💰

Schlafly's Stop ERA campaign (1970s): mobilised working-class women against ERA — argued it would eliminate protections and force women into combat. Conservative women as organised political force opposing feminist agenda. Evangelical Christian women: anti-feminist movement from 1970s. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Influence in Government
facts: Division undermined lobbying effectiveness: competing women's organisations with different priorities weakened political voice. Middle-class suffragists and working-class labour activists rarely coordinated. NOW vs radical feminist groups: moderate vs radical tactics debate replicated suffrage-era divisions. 💥

Schlafly's movement explicitly targeted at reversing feminist influence in government. Religious Right from 1970s: gave anti-feminist agenda organisational base. Conservative women's organisations lobbied successfully against ERA, abortion rights and sex education. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Education
facts: Class division: middle-class campaigns for higher education access did not prioritise working-class women's immediate needs. Hull House: middle-class women sometimes patronising toward immigrant communities. Divisions limited scope of educational demands to middle-class priorities. 💥 💰

Conservative opposition to Title IX: male sports establishment and conservative women argued against co-educational sports. Religious conservatives opposed sex education and reproductive health education. Anti-feminist backlash targeted feminist curriculum changes and women's studies programmes. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Attitudes and Culture
facts: Class divisions: flapper culture — urban, white, middle-class. Rural, working-class, Black and immigrant women unaffected or hostile. Temperance: middle-class moral imposition on working-class cultures that resented interference. Radical feminism (1970s): alienated moderates — 'Radicalesbians' and 'abolition of marriage' groups provoked backlash. 💥 💰

Race divisions: radical feminist movement of 1960s–70s criticised as predominantly white and middle-class — excluded Black women's concerns. NOW slow to incorporate racial justice. Schlafly's cultural conservatism: traditional family values as women's liberation from feminist pressure. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Reproductive Rights
facts: Conservative women's opposition: National Right to Life Committee included many women as members and leaders. Conservative Catholic and evangelical women: religious conviction that abortion was wrong. Schlafly: ERA would force women into combat — actively mobilised women against feminist agenda. 💥 💭

Race divisions within feminist movement: Black feminists criticised reproductive rights campaigns as focused on white middle-class concerns — ignoring sterilisation abuse against Black and Native women. Class divisions: Hyde Amendment most affected low-income women — those with least representation in feminist movement. 💥

subheadings.label: Employment and Wages
facts: Class divisions: middle-class professional women vs working-class factory workers — different priorities. Professional women wanted access to high-paid careers; working-class women needed immediate wage increases and safety. WTUL and NOW rarely coordinated effectively. 💥 💰

Schlafly mobilised working-class women against ERA by arguing it would remove protective legislation. Conservative opposition to equal pay legislation: argued market should set wages. Race divisions: Black and minority women earned less than white women — feminist movement slow to address compounded race-gender pay discrimination. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Unions and Labour
facts: Class divisions most acute in union context: middle-class suffragists rarely prioritised labour rights. Lawrence Strike (1912) received no suffragist support. Working-class women's labour campaigns received no middle-class feminist support. Trade union male leadership excluded women while middle-class women's organisations focused on suffrage not wages. 💥 💰

Ideological divisions within labour movement: AFL vs CIO on women's inclusion. CLUW (1974) had to fight for recognition within male-dominated AFL-CIO. Conservative opposition to minimum wage, equal pay and union rights legislation consistently defeated attempts to raise economic floor for women workers. 💥 💭

subheadings.label: Property and Legal Rights
facts: ERA battle most stark example of division: women who had campaigned 50 years for constitutional equality opposed by women like Schlafly who argued ERA would harm women. Conservative women as organised legal opposition. Religious conservative legal organisations challenged Title IX and sex discrimination legislation. 💥 💭

Race divisions in legal campaigns: mainstream feminist legal organisations focused on white women's legal concerns. Black women's specific vulnerabilities — sterilisation abuse, welfare discrimination — rarely prioritised. Class divisions: legal aid for poor women inadequate — legal gains benefited those who could afford lawyers. ERA's failure the ultimate result of these divisions. 💥

obstacleKey: 🦅 Federal Government · 💭 Attitudes in Society · 💥 Division and Conservative Opposition
